title: Host
text: Many PocketBase instances behind one listener, routed by hostname. Each request's hostname picks an instance, the request passes the gates (such as the firewall), and one runtime provider serves it: pocker runs instances in-process, docker runs each in its own container. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Host
heading: Install
text: Host is built into pocketone . It takes over serve when pocketone.yaml names a provider ; without one, pocketone serve runs a single app as usual. provider: pocker # or docker In your own Go build, register the providers you link, build the host from the config and run it. examples/pocketone/multi.go is the stock binary's version: host.RegisterProvider(&pocker.Provider{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}) h, err := host.FromConfig(host.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}) if errors.Is(err, host.ErrNoProvider) { // no provider in pocketone.yaml: serve a single app instead } err = h.Run(ctx) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/host .

title: Host
heading: Configure
text: A host reads these pocketone.yaml sections: provider: pocker # which runtime provider runs the instances server: https: ":443" # the main address http: ":80" # redirects to https (alone: serves plain HTTP) plain: [":8080"] # extra plain-HTTP addresses, no redirect (e.g. a private network) tls: { cert: cert.pem, key: key.pem } # reloaded when the files change; or the autotls section instances: file: ./instances.yaml # where the instances come from dev: false # also serve unknown hostnames pocker: { root: ./pb_root } # the provider's own section (pocker or docker) firewall: { allow_cidrs: [10.0.0.0/8] } # any gate's section turns that gate on provider and server belong to Config. With no https or http , the host listens on 127.0.0.1:8090 . The instances section is this plugin's (keys below). In production the instances file is required; with dev: true it's optional. The app section is for a single app and is refused when a provider is set: each instance has its own folder under the provider's root.

title: Host
heading: instances:
text: Where a multi-instance host's instances come from (a YAML file), and dev mode (serve unknown hostnames). file string instances.yaml The instances file (id, hosts and settings for each instance), reloaded when it changes. dev bool Also serve unknown hostnames: each becomes an instance named after it, in dev mode, with its folder made on first use.

title: Host
heading: The instances file
text: instances: id: blog # also the folder name: /blog hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # the app's environment, seen by its JS hooks encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # encrypts PocketBase's stored settings access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] } limits: { max_js_execution: 60s } # over the provider's defaults plugins: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } } # settings for plugins, by name id: old hosts: [old.example.com] blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" } The file is checked for changes every 2 seconds; edits apply without restarting the host. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. Other fields: version and runtime (which release or provider runs it), dir (another folder), dev , superusers (pocker upserts them when the app starts), private (for host Go code, never seen by JS) and remote (another server runs it).

title: Host
heading: What a request gets
text: A hostname no instance maps gets 404, and no folder is created. In dev mode it becomes a new instance named after the hostname, in PocketBase dev mode. A blocked instance answers every request with its status and message. An instance with remote set is forwarded there after the gates (a plain proxy to the URL, or Edge for a fleet). GET /_pocker/health on any hostname reports the host's status, how many instances it knows and how many are running.

title: Host
heading: Switching provider
text: Switching between pocker and docker is a config change: both keep instances in / . Stop the containers first when leaving docker (they keep running across a host restart on purpose). Data only moves forward: an instance started on a newer PocketBase than wrote its data is upgraded.

title: Host
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Runtime provider: every instance runs in this process ( provider: pocker ). Docker Runtime provider: each instance runs in its own container ( provider: docker ). Firewall A gate: peer allow-list, client IPs and rate limits. On when the config has firewall or rate_limits . Edge Forwards requests for instances another edge runs (the edges section). Mothership Its mirror replaces the instances file as the instance source, and lists the other edges. Auto TLS Certificates for the main listener, issued for the hostnames instances map. Lifecycle Measures disk use and last request for each instance. Server Timing Server-Timing headers for each step of a request.

title: Host
heading: Building on Host
text: Runtime provider. Implement host.Provider ( Name , Prepare ) and call host.RegisterProvider ; provider: picks it by name. Prepare sets h.Runtime , a host.Runtime ( Name , Serves , ServeInstance , Ready ), with optional Prechecker , Syncer , Statser and Shutdowner . Instance source. Implement host.InstanceSource ( Snapshot , Watch ) to feed instances from anywhere, such as a control plane, and pass it as host.Options.Source . YAMLSource is the built-in one. Gates. A host.Gate checks the peer ( AllowPeer ) and admits each request ( Admit ). RegisterSectionGate turns one on from its own config sections, as the firewall does; ClientIPResolver passes the real client IP on to the app. Forwarding. host.Options.Forward serves requests for instances with remote set (Edge fills it). Listeners and wrappers. Host.TLS takes a TLSProvider , Host.Wrappers wrap the whole handler, and Host.Background runs jobs until shutdown. Per-instance settings. A plugin reads its own plugins. with inst.PluginConfig(name) and host.DecodePluginConfig .

title: Host
heading: Example
text: A toy host: instances from a YAML file, served by a runtime that answers with the instance it resolved. Run it from this folder with go run ./example --instances instances.yaml , then curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/ . // A minimal host: instances from a YAML file, routed by hostname, served by a toy runtime that answers with the // instance it resolved. Real hosts plug in a provider instead (ext/pocker in-process, ext/docker in containers). // // go run ./example --instances instances.yaml // curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/ package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "net/http" "os" "os/signal" "syscall" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/host" ) type echoRuntime struct{} func (echoRuntime) Name() string { return "echo" } func (echoRuntime) Serves(inst host.Instance) bool { return true } func (echoRuntime) Ready() bool { return true } func (echoRuntime) ServeInstance(w http.ResponseWriter, r http.Request, inst host.Instance) { fmt.Fprintf(w, "instance %s (%s%s)\n", inst.ID, r.Host, r.URL.Path) } func main() { instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file: instances: [{id: blog, hosts: [blog.localhost]}]") listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address") flag.Parse() ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() h := &host.Host{Source: &host.YAMLSource{Path: instances}, Runtime: echoRuntime{}, Listeners: host.Listeners{Listen: listen}} if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err) os.Exit(1) } }

title: Host
heading: How it works
text: Instance , InstanceSource , YAMLSource The instance model and where instances come from. Directory Instances by hostname and id, kept current from the source. Handler Health path, peer check, hostname, blocked, then remote (the Forward hook) or local (the runtime), with the gates. Runtime What a provider implements. Exactly one per process. Gate , RegisterSectionGate , ChainGates Request gates. Serve , TLSProvider Listeners: plain, TLS (a provider such as autotls, or cert files reloaded on change), redirect, graceful shutdown. Host , FromConfig All of the above assembled, by hand or from pocketone.yaml .

Mail Trap Dev mode: mail from an app without SMTP lands in a built-in inbox. Dev Users Local testing only: a superuser and a user with password "password". JS Embed JS hooks and migrations embedded in the binary.

title: JS Embed
text: Ship a plugin's or app's JS hooks and migrations inside the binary, instead of pb_hooks and pb_migrations on disk. Nothing is written to disk and nothing on disk can override them. PocketHost's mothership binary uses it for its own hooks. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: JS Embed
heading: Install
text: JS Embed is not in the pocketone binary. Add it to your own Go build: embed the folder and pass it to jsvm as an extension. //go:embed hooks var files embed.FS hooks, _ := fs.Sub(files, "hooks") jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{jsembed.Hooks(hooks), jsembed.Migrations(migrations)}, }) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsembed .

title: JS Embed
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen. You choose what to embed in Go: jsembed.Hooks(fsys) : the .pb.js files at the root of fsys . jsvm's HooksDir is then ignored and hook watching is off. jsembed.Migrations(fsys) : the migration files at the root of fsys . MigrationsDir is then ignored. List only the half you embed; the other stays on disk.

title: JS Embed
heading: Use
text: Put your .pb.js files at the root of the embedded folder, and shared modules in subfolders (for example lib/ ). Load a shared module with require(__hooks + "/lib/x.js") . Inside that module, require("./y.js") stays in the embedded folder, and a relative require from a .pb.js handler resolves under __hooks . Rebuild the binary to change a hook. There's no watching and no restart on edit. What doesn't work, on purpose: .. escapes, absolute disk paths and node_modules lookups are "module not found". JS that reads files itself ( $os.readFile(__hooks + ...) ) gets "no such file": __hooks is the virtual path /pb_embedded/pb_hooks , never looked up on disk. A real folder at that path makes no difference.

title: JS Embed
heading: Integrations
text: jsvm extensions. Hooks and Migrations are jsvm.Extension s, so they sit in jsvm.Config.Extensions next to other extensions such as JS Errors. Building on it. jsembed.Root is the value of __hooks with embedded hooks. Any fs.FS works, not only embed.FS : a zip, an overlay, or a test's fstest.MapFS .

title: JS Embed
heading: Example
text: example/main.go serves a route from hooks embedded in the binary, with no pb_hooks folder on disk. Run go run ./example serve from this folder, then curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello . The hook is example/hooks/main.pb.js ; it requires example/hooks/lib/greet.js . // Command example serves its JS hooks from files embedded in the binary: no pb_hooks folder on disk. // // go run ./example serve // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello package main import ( "embed" "io/fs" "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/plugins/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsembed" ) //go:embed hooks var files embed.FS func main() { hooks, err := fs.Sub(files, "hooks") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{jsembed.Hooks(hooks)}}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

text: Hooks and Migrations implement jsvm's HookFiles , Require and MigrationFiles extension methods, PocketOne's small seam in jsvm; with no extensions, jsvm behaves like upstream. The require registry joins and cleans paths as text (no symlinks, no disk) and serves only paths under __hooks from the FS. It used to live inside jsvm ( HooksFS / MigrationsFS ); it moved here on 2026-11-13.

title: JS Errors
text: JS hook errors that point at the .pb.js file they come from. When a hook in pb_hooks throws, the error says pb_hooks/main.pb.js:12:3 instead of /your/cwd/pb.js:1:40 , so you can go straight to the line. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: JS Errors
heading: Install
text: JS Errors is built into pocketone and always on . There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, list it in the JS VM's extensions: app := pocketbase.New() jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{jserrors.New()}}) app.Start() The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jserrors .

title: JS Errors
heading: Configure
text: There is nothing to configure. It works on whatever hooks folder the app uses ( --hooksDir , or app.hooks_dir in pocketone.yaml ).

title: JS Errors
heading: Use
text: Write hooks as usual. When one fails, the error in the log names the hooks file, line and column. For example, this hook: // pb_hooks/main.pb.js routerAdd("GET", "/boom", (e) = { const order = null return e.json(200, { total: order.total }) }) logs an error at pb_hooks/main.pb.js:4:... when you open /boom , not at pb.js:1:... . What it covers: errors thrown by handlers you register in a hooks file: hooks, routes, middlewares and cron jobs; errors while a hooks file itself runs at startup (the file is named in the startup error). The file is named after your hooks folder: with --hooksDir ./hooks , errors say hooks/main.pb.js:4:3 . A handler it can't place, such as one built from a string or registered at runtime, keeps the original message. To try it, run the example: cd example && go run . serve --dev curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/boom and read the log.

title: JS Errors
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Built in for every instance: hook errors in each instance's log name pb_hooks/ : : . jsembed Combine the two, for example Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{jsembed.Hooks(hooks), jserrors.New()} . Embedded files are named pb_hooks/ .

title: JS Errors
heading: Building on JS Errors
text: It's a plain JS VM extension, so it sits next to any other extension in jsvm.Config.Extensions . The errors it rewrites still unwrap to the original error, so Go code that checks for a goja.Exception with errors.As keeps working. It has no Go API beyond jserrors.New() .

title: JS Errors
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs an app next to example/pb_hooks ; request /boom in dev mode and the logged error names pb_hooks/main.pb.js:4 . // Command example shows hook errors pointing at the .pb.js file: run it in dev mode next to example/pb_hooks and // request /boom; the logged error names pb_hooks/main.pb.js:4:... instead of /pb.js:1:... // // cd example && go run . serve --dev // curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/boom package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/plugins/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jserrors" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{jserrors.New()}}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: JS Errors
heading: How it works
text: The JS VM turns each hook handler back into source ( fn.toString() ) and compiles it again as its own program under /pb.js . That name also anchors relative require() calls, so it can't change, and errors carry it. This plugin: remembers each hooks file while it loads, and where each handler sits in it; rewrites pb.js: : in errors those handlers throw to pb_hooks/ : : (the wrapped error still unwraps to the original); names the file in errors raised while a hooks file itself runs. It's a jsvm extension ( jsvm.Config.Extensions ) with OnLoad and OnCompile methods, plus jsvm.ScriptPath() , PocketOne's small seam in the JS VM. With no extensions, the JS VM behaves like PocketBase's. It used to live inside the JS VM ( hooksource.go ) and moved here on 2026-11-13.

title: Lifecycle
text: Looks after the data of the instances a host serves. Today it measures facts about each instance (disk used, last request served) and reports them. Later it will also carry out decisions about that data, such as archiving. Status. Working, first step: facts and the measure decision. Archiving, restoring, offloading backups and purging come next, as further decisions. The rules engine is ready as a Go library but isn't read from pocketone.yaml yet. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Lifecycle
heading: Install
text: Lifecycle runs on a host that serves many instances (ext/host, with pocker or docker), not on a single app. The stock pocketone binary turns it on by itself in host mode: when pocketone.yaml names a provider ( pocker or docker ), every instance under that provider's root folder is measured. There's no switch to flip. provider: pocker # or docker instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } In your own host build, add it as a gate (to see requests) and a background job: lc := &lifecycle.Lifecycle{Directory: h.Directory, Folder: func(i host.Instance) string { return filepath.Join(root, i.ID) }} h.Gates = append(h.Gates, lc) // records each local instance's last request h.Background = append(h.Background, lc.Run) // measures and reports on the policy's schedule Folder says where an instance's data lives. The stock binary uses the instance's own dir when it has one, else / .

title: Lifecycle
heading: Configure
text: The lifecycle section in pocketone.yaml sets the schedule. Everything is optional. lifecycle: measure_every: 24h # how old a disk measurement may get report_every: 1h # how often changed last-request times are reported concurrency: 2 # instances measured at once

title: Lifecycle
heading: The policy
text: What to do comes from a policy. The built-in one ( YAMLPolicy ) reads this section and decides one thing: measure an instance when it was never measured, or when its measurement is older than measure_every . Zero or missing values fall back to the defaults. Rules with criteria, all / any / not , vetoes and budgets exist in the rules engine, but the lifecycle section doesn't take them yet.

title: Lifecycle
heading: lifecycle:
text: Instance data on this host: how often disk use is measured and last-request times are reported. measure_every duration 24h0m0s How old an instance's disk measurement may get before it is measured again. Default 24h. report_every duration 1h0m0s How often changed last-request times are reported to the sink. Default 1h. concurrency int 2 How many instances are measured at once. Default 2.

title: Lifecycle
heading: What it measures
text: For each instance this host serves itself (not the ones it forwards to another edge): disk_bytes : the size of the regular files in the instance's folder (symlinks aren't followed; 0 when there's no folder), and measured_at , when that was measured. last_active : the last request this host served for it, recorded at most once a minute per instance.

title: Lifecycle
heading: When
text: As soon as the instance list loads, every instance is measured, because none has been measured yet. After that it checks once a minute and measures the instances whose measurement is older than measure_every . Changed last-request times are reported every report_every . Facts are kept in memory. With the default log sink, a restart measures everything again.

title: Lifecycle
heading: What you'll see
text: Log lines from the default sink and the measuring pass: INFO lifecycle: facts instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 INFO lifecycle: measured instances=12 disk_bytes=48213504 ms=37 lifecycle: facts is each report the sink receives (after a measuring pass, and for last-request times). lifecycle: measured follows a measuring pass, with how long it took. Problems show as warnings: lifecycle: measuring (a folder couldn't be read), lifecycle: report (the sink failed; last-request times are retried next time) and lifecycle: policy .

title: Lifecycle
heading: Try it
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints each instance's size: go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml

title: Lifecycle
heading: Works with
text: Host Lifecycle is a host.Gate (it sees each request to record last_active ) and a host background job ( Run ). It lists instances from host.Directory . Pocker Instances under pocker.root (default ./pb_root ), one folder per instance. Docker Instances under docker.root , the same / layout. It knows nothing about plans, payments or tenants: that belongs to whichever policy provider is configured.

title: Lifecycle
heading: Your own policy
text: Set Lifecycle.Policy to anything that implements PolicyProvider : type PolicyProvider interface { Decide(ctx context.Context, facts []Facts) ([]Decision, error) // what to do now, and why ReportEvery() time.Duration // how often last-request times are reported Concurrency() int // instances worked on at once } A control plane can provide its own, for example one that delegates the decisions to a mothership, and providers can wrap each other. Only the measure action is carried out today; any other action is logged as lifecycle: action not supported yet .

title: Lifecycle
heading: Your own sink
text: Set Lifecycle.Sink to anything that implements Sink ( Report(ctx, facts []Facts) error ) to send facts somewhere other than the log. A sink that also implements Loader ( Load(ctx) ([]Facts, error) ) gives the facts back at start, so a restart doesn't measure everything again or forget last-request times.

title: Lifecycle
heading: Rules: criteria an app can replace
text: rules (package github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/lifecycle/rules , standard library only) is the engine policies are built from, on an edge or a mothership. A subject is whatever the caller evaluates: an instance's facts on an edge, an account with its instances on a mothership. Criteria answer one question about a subject (stale? orphaned? over its plan?) and say why. They live in a Registry by name: an app registers its own or replaces a built-in one ( Register("stale", ...) ), and every rule that refers to the name ( Ref("stale") ) follows, so what "stale" means is the app's to decide. Where they come from is pluggable too: code, or definitions from config ( Load ) built from kinds the app registered ( RegisterKind("idle", ...) ) and combined with all , any and not . A YAML section and a mothership are both just sources of definitions. Load registers nothing when a definition is wrong. Rules lead from a criterion to an action, with named vetoes that always win and a budget per run. Reports list each decision with its reasons, what was vetoed and by what, what the budget held back and what failed. Summary gives one line per rule ( archive-stale: 3 decided, 1 vetoed ). Evaluating does nothing by itself: acting on the decisions, or only logging them in a dry run, is the caller's. A definition, as config would supply it: stale: { kind: idle, params: { after: 8760h } } archivable: { kind: all, of: [stale, free_plan] } keep: { kind: not, of: [archivable] } And in Go: r := rules.NewRegistryFacts r.RegisterKind("idle", idleFor) // params: { after: 8760h } _ = r.Load(map[string]rules.Def{ "stale": {Kind: "idle", Params: map[string]any{"after": "8760h"}}, "archivable": {Kind: "all", Of: []string{"stale", "free_plan"}}, }) e := rules.Engine[Facts]{Key: id, Rules: []rules.Rule[Facts]{{ Name: "archive-stale", Action: "archive", When: r.Ref("archivable"), Unless: []rules.Veto[Facts]{{Name: "pinned", If: r.Ref("pinned")}}, Budget: 200, }}} report := e.Evaluate(ctx, facts) Every rule sees every subject, so one subject can get several decisions. Make rules exclusive by building them from exclusive criteria.

title: Lifecycle
heading: Example
text: example/main.go measures the instance folders under a root once and prints their facts, which is what a host's lifecycle does daily. // Measure the instance folders under a root once and print their facts (what a host's lifecycle does daily). // // go run ./example --root ./pb_root --instances instances.yaml package main import ( "context" "flag" "fmt" "log" "log/slog" "path/filepath" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/host" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/lifecycle" ) func main() { root := flag.String("root", "./pb_root", "one folder per instance: / ") instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file") flag.Parse() src := &host.YAMLSource{Path: instances, Required: true} list, err := src.Snapshot(context.Background()) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } dir := host.NewDirectory(slog.Default()) dir.Load(list) lc := &lifecycle.Lifecycle{ Directory: dir, Folder: func(i host.Instance) string { if i.Dir != "" { return i.Dir } return filepath.Join( root, i.ID) }, Sink: lifecycle.LogSink{}, } lc.Step(context.Background()) // never measured: every instance is measured now for _, f := range lc.Local() { fmt.Printf("%-24s %12d bytes\n", f.Instance, f.DiskBytes) } }

title: Lifecycle
heading: How it works
text: Go module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/lifecycle . The stock binary wires it in examples/pocketone/multi.go . Run loads recorded facts from a Loader sink, then waits for the host's instance list to load (checking every second). From then on, once a minute, it asks the policy for decisions on the current facts, measures the instances it was asked to ( concurrency at a time) and reports what it measured to the sink. Measuring walks the folder and adds up regular file sizes. An instance's pending last-request time goes out with its measurement, so it isn't reported twice. Admit records last_active only for instances this host serves itself ( Remote empty), and never refuses a request.

title: Mail Relay
text: Outgoing mail for Pocker instances that haven't set up SMTP. Stock PocketBase falls back to the host's sendmail when SMTP is off. Under Pocker that would run sendmail on the shared host for every tenant. With this plugin: SMTP on in an instance's Settings → Mail: PocketBase sends the mail itself. Bring your own SMTP always wins. SMTP off: the mail goes through your relay as @ , within per-instance limits. sendmail never runs. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Relay
heading: Install
text: Mail Relay is not in the pocketone binary. Add it to the plugins of your own Pocker build, with your sending domain and relay: srv.Plugins = append(srv.Plugins, mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.example.com", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: "smtp.provider.com:587", Username: "…", Password: "…"}, })) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailrelay . It works the same in pocker.Provider{Plugins: ...} . It also registers on a single app, but a single app can set up its own SMTP and doesn't need a relay.

title: Mail Relay
heading: The relay (Go)
text: Domain and Upstream are required; the host doesn't start without them. Domain : every relayed message is From @Domain . Upstream : what delivers the mail. SMTPUpstream ships here: Addr (host:port), optional Username and Password (PLAIN auth, only over TLS or to localhost), ImplicitTLS for port 465 (otherwise STARTTLS when the server offers it), and Timeout (default 30 s). It dials with its own dialer, so Pocker's egress rules for tenants (public addresses only) don't block a relay on a private address. Anything with Send(ctx, from, to, raw) works, for example an Amazon SES SendRawEmail sender. LocalPart : picks an instance's address from its id. The default is the first label of the id, lowercased: blog.localhost → blog . Limits: PerMinute (default 20) and Daily (default 200) per instance, MaxRecipients (To + Cc + Bcc, default 5) and MaxSize (encoded message, default 1 MiB) per message.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Defaults for every instance (pocketone.yaml)
text: mailrelay: { per_minute: 20, daily: 200 } Limits set in Go win over this section. Each instance can override it (see Per-instance settings).

title: Mail Relay
heading: Use
text: Once it's in, there's nothing to run. Each instance's mail is relayed whenever its SMTP is off. Settings → Mail in an instance's dashboard shows its superusers the relay: the address it sends as, its limits and how many messages it sent today. When sending is off for the instance, it says so and points to the SMTP settings. The instance's log gets one line per message, with masked addresses: mail from blog@… to a @x.org accepted . Refusals and upstream failures are logged too. A refused message returns an error to whoever triggered the mail, such as a password-reset request: sending off, too many recipients, too large, or the limit reached.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Works with
text: Pocker The host it's built for. Every instance gets the relay, its own address and its own limits. Mail Trap In development, point SMTPUpstream at the trap's SMTP port and every relayed message lands in one inbox, tagged with the instance. The example below does this. Bulk Mail Campaigns go through PocketBase's mailer by default, so with SMTP off they are relayed and count against the instance's limits.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: Each instance can override the defaults in its plugins.mailrelay settings, from instances.yaml or your instance source (for example, per plan): instances: id: free-plan-app plugins: { mailrelay: { send: false } } # refuse its mail unless it uses its own SMTP id: big-app plugins: { mailrelay: { per_minute: 60, daily: 2000 } } A change to these settings restarts the instance's app on its next request. Use send: false , not enabled: false , to stop an instance sending. enabled: false turns the plugin off for that instance, and with SMTP off PocketBase then falls back to the host's sendmail . Don't set it under Pocker.

title: Mail Relay
heading: Building on Mail Relay
text: Your own upstream. Implement mailrelay.Upstream ( Send(ctx, from, to, raw) ) to deliver through an API. Your own hooks first. The relay runs after the app's own onMailerSend hooks, so they can still change or drop a message. Go API. ( mailrelay.Plugin).Address(id) returns the From address an instance sends as. REST API (superusers): GET /api/mailrelay returns the instance's relay status: active , send , address , perMinute , daily , sentToday .

title: Mail Relay
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs a Pocker host whose relay sends to the dev mail trap, so every instance's mail lands in one inbox at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Run go run ./example --dev from this folder, then trigger a password reset on any instance: curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com Log in to an instance's dashboard as admin@example.com / password to see the relay on Settings → Mail. --listen changes the instances' port; PB_MAILTRAP_HTTP and PB_MAILTRAP_SMTP change the trap's. // Command example is a Pocker build with mailrelay, relaying into PocketOne's dev mail trap: every instance // without its own SMTP sends as @mail.localhost, and all of it lands in one inbox. // // go run ./example --dev // // Then trigger mail on any instance, for example a password reset (each instance has the test user below): // // curl -X POST http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // curl -X POST http://beta.localhost:8090/api/collections/users/request-password-reset -d email=user@example.com // // and read it in PocketOne's dev mail trap at http://127.0.0.1:8025 (filter by instance; PB_MAILTRAP_HTTP and // PB_MAILTRAP_SMTP change its ports). Settings → Mail in each dashboard shows the relay. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "context" "flag" "log" "os" "os/signal" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailrelay" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker" ) func main() { dev := flag.Bool("dev", false, "serve any hostname (alpha.localhost, beta.localhost, ...); otherwise instances.yaml is required") listen := flag.String("listen", "", "HTTP address for the instances (default :8090)") flag.Parse() cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig() cfg.Dev = cfg.Dev dev if listen != "" { cfg.Listen = listen } ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt) defer stop() // The dev mail trap (ext/mailtrap) stands in for the operator's real relay (SES, a provider's SMTP, ...) inbox, err := mailtrap.Default("mailrelay example: the relay sends to the trap") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } srv := &pocker.Server{ Config: cfg, Plugins: []pocker.Plugin{ mailrelay.New(mailrelay.Config{ Domain: "mail.localhost", Upstream: mailrelay.SMTPUpstream{Addr: inbox.SMTPAddr}, }), }, // local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" SetupApp: func(_ pocker.Instance, app core.App) error { return devusers.Ensure(app) }, } if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Mail Relay
heading: How it works
text: The plugin binds PocketBase's OnMailerSend on every instance, last, after the app's own hooks. No core change. When SMTP is off it doesn't call e.Next() , so PocketBase's sendmail fallback never runs. It relays the message in-process instead. Nothing is written to the instance's settings. A backup restored somewhere else has no relay credentials in it, and falls back to stock PocketBase behavior. For each message: Check it's allowed. May this instance send ( send )? Are there no more than 5 recipients (To + Cc + Bcc)? Is the encoded size no more than 1 MiB? Count it. Each message counts once against the instance's limits, however many recipients it has. The day resets at midnight UTC. Counts are kept in memory. Set the sender. The From address becomes @ . The display name is kept, minus anything that looks like an address or a link. The app's own sender address becomes Reply-To , unless it's PocketBase's @example.com placeholder. Build and send. Bcc stays out of the headers. An X-Pocker-Instance header is added, then the message goes to the Upstream . Log it to the instance's own log.

title: Mail Trap
text: A development mail catcher (like MailDev or Mailpit) for testing a plugin or app that sends mail. In dev mode, an app whose SMTP is off sends its mail here instead of the host's sendmail , and you read it at http://127.0.0.1:8025. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mail Trap
heading: Install
text: Mail Trap is built into pocketone , for a single app and for every instance under provider: pocker . There's nothing to install: run pocketone serve --dev with SMTP off and it's active. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() mailtrap.MustRegister(app) app.Start() Under Pocker, add mailtrap.New() to the plugins. The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap .

title: Mail Trap
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section or settings screen. It turns itself on only when both are true: the app is in dev mode ( serve --dev , or a dev instance under Pocker), and the app's SMTP is off (Settings → Mail). Turn SMTP on, or run without --dev , and it does nothing. Two environment variables move its ports: PB_MAILTRAP_HTTP 127.0.0.1:8025 (the web inbox) PB_MAILTRAP_SMTP 127.0.0.1:1025 (SMTP) Never expose these ports: anyone who can reach them can read the mail.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Use
text: Start the app with --dev . It prints the inbox address once it's active. Make your plugin or app send mail: a verification, a password reset, $app.newMailClient() , a bulk mail campaign. Each caught message is also printed as one line in the terminal. Open http://127.0.0.1:8025. The list refreshes every 2 seconds. Click a message to see it as HTML , Text or Raw source. Clear empties the inbox. It keeps the last 500 messages, in memory only; they're gone when the process exits. If its ports are taken, it still catches mail and prints each message in the terminal.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Works with
text: Pocker One inbox for every dev instance. Each message is labeled with the instance that sent it (its X-Pocker-Instance header), and the inbox filters by instance. Mail Relay Mail Relay's example uses the trap's SMTP port as its relay, so relayed mail goes through the real SMTP path and lands here. Bulk Mail In dev mode with SMTP off, campaign mail lands in the inbox instead of being sent.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Building on Mail Trap
text: Its hook runs last. It binds OnMailerSend after the app's own hooks, so your onMailerSend hooks still run and can change the message first. When it takes a message it never calls the next handler, so sendmail never runs. SMTP for other tools. The SMTP listener accepts any message (and any AUTH), so anything that speaks SMTP can send to it. Go API. mailtrap.Default(reason) returns the process-wide trap, starting it on first use. A Trap has Messages() , Clear() , Add(from, to, raw, label) and AddMessage(msg, label) , and Handler() serves the inbox. Trap{SMTPAddr, HTTPAddr}.Start(ctx) runs a separate trap, for example in a test. Inbox API. GET /api/messages (newest first, without bodies), GET /api/messages/{id} , GET /api/messages/{id}/raw (.eml) and DELETE /api/messages , on the inbox address.

title: Mail Trap
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app in dev mode with the trap. Run go run ./example serve --dev from this folder, request a password reset for user@example.com (password password ) from the dashboard (log in as admin@example.com / password ), and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // Command example runs one app in dev mode with the dev mail trap: request a password reset for user@example.com // in the dashboard and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025. // // go run ./example serve --dev package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) mailtrap.MustRegister(app) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: MCP
text: A Model Context Protocol endpoint at /mcp , so an agent (Claude Code, a Claude connector, any Streamable HTTP client) can work with your app. No sidecar process. Every tool is one REST call, run as the caller. A tool call becomes a request to your app's own API, made in-process as whoever signed in. API rules, request hooks, middleware and rate limits apply because it is the REST request. MCP makes no permission decisions of its own. The whole stock API is built in as pb_ tools (records, files, auth, collections, settings, logs, crons, SQL, backups). An app that only uses the stock API needs nothing else. Your own endpoints get tools the same way: write the REST endpoint, then the tool wrapper ( $mcp.addEndpoint in pb_hooks , or AddEndpoint from Go). Sign-in with OAuth through OAuth Server: add https:// /mcp to Claude and sign in in a browser, as a superuser or an app user. The connection stays signed in until you revoke it. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: MCP
heading: Install
text: MCP is built into pocketone and always on, with Tokens and OAuth Server for sign-in and $mcp in pb_hooks . There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts. Register Tokens and OAuth Server too for OAuth sign-in, and bind $mcp into the JS hooks if you use them: app := pocketbase.New() tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) oauthserver.MustRegister(app, oauthserver.Config{}) mcp.MustRegister(app, mcp.Config{}) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(vm goja.Runtime) { mcp.BindJS(vm, app) }}) app.Start() The order doesn't matter: MCP picks its sign-in on serve, and tools that pb_hooks declare before mcp.Register wait for it. The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mcp .

title: MCP
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag, environment variable or settings screen for MCP. In pocketone it serves /mcp with every built-in tool, and: anyone who can sign in through OAuth Server can connect: superusers and app users of any auth collection, each with their own rights; an agent's connection doesn't expire; it lasts until you revoke it; the server's name for clients comes from Settings → Application → Application name . A Go build can change the path, the tools, the caps and the sign-in (see Go config).

title: MCP
heading: Scopes
text: MCP registers no scopes of its own. When an agent connects, the consent page offers Full access (the account's rights, like a PocketBase auth token) or Only these , with a box for each of your token scopes (scopes that only reach /_pocker/ routes, like deploy , aren't offered unless the client asks for them). The protected resource metadata lists the same scopes in scopes_supported , so a client can ask for some up front; the user can still change the ticks. A connection limited to scopes is held to them exactly like an API token with those scopes on the REST API: Each tool call is checked against the scopes' paths and methods (or Match guards). A request they don't cover is refused with 403 , and the tool returns that as an error. Collection rules see only those scopes in @request.headers.x_token_scope_ . tools/list hides tools none of the scopes reaches, and the instructions name the scopes. The token itself still works only on /mcp . To limit an agent further, sign it in as an account with fewer rights.

title: MCP
heading: Behind a proxy
text: The OAuth resource URL must match the URL clients use. MCP builds it from the request's host, taking the scheme from Settings → Application URL when its host is the same, else from TLS or X-Forwarded-Proto . If your proxy rewrites the host, set Config.PublicURL in a Go build.

title: MCP
heading: Browsers
text: Requests with an Origin header from another site get 403 . Clients that send no Origin , such as Claude's servers and Claude Code, pass. A Go build can allow more origins with Config.AllowedOrigins .

title: MCP
heading: Connect Claude Code
text: claude mcp add --transport http my-app https:// /mcp claude mcp login my-app # or /mcp in a session A browser opens on your app's sign-in page. Sign in (as an app user, or with Sign in as a superuser ), check what the consent page says and click Allow . Claude and Claude Code can connect without registering, through their published client metadata documents. For a Claude connector, add https:// /mcp as a custom connector and sign in the same way. Other MCP clients register themselves with your app first.

title: MCP
heading: Paste a token instead
text: A PocketBase auth token, or an API token not bound to any resource, works on /mcp as it does on the REST API, and tool calls forward it unchanged. A scoped API token works only if one of its scopes covers /mcp ; to limit an agent to scopes, connect it through the consent page instead (see Scopes).

title: MCP
heading: Who a tool call runs as
text: Whoever signed in. A superuser gets what the API gives superusers; an app user gets what your collection rules give them. Superuser-only tools are left out of other callers' tool list (that's presentation; the endpoint still decides).

title: MCP
heading: See and revoke connected agents
text: Each sign-in creates an API token bound to /mcp , named " (OAuth)". They're listed under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label; click Revoke to disconnect an agent.

title: MCP
heading: Built-in tools
text: One per stock endpoint: health pb_check_health everyone records pb_list_records ( perPage 20 by default), pb_get_record , pb_create_record , pb_update_record , pb_delete_record , pb_run_batch per collection rules auth pb_list_auth_methods , pb_request_otp , pb_request_verification , pb_confirm_verification , pb_request_password_reset , pb_confirm_password_reset , pb_request_email_change , pb_confirm_email_change per collection files pb_download_file (protected files through a file token made as the caller; images as images, text as text, others as embedded data; up to 10 MB) per view rules collections pb_list_collections , pb_get_collection , pb_create_collection , pb_update_collection , pb_delete_collection , pb_truncate_collection , pb_import_collections , pb_get_collection_scaffolds , pb_list_oauth2_providers , pb_dry_run_view superusers settings pb_get_settings , pb_update_settings , pb_test_s3 , pb_test_email , pb_generate_apple_client_secret superusers logs pb_list_logs , pb_get_log , pb_get_log_stats , pb_truncate_logs superusers crons pb_list_crons , pb_run_cron superusers sql pb_run_sql superusers backups pb_list_backups , pb_create_backup , pb_upload_backup , pb_download_backup , pb_delete_backup , pb_restore_backup superusers Record create and update take field values in data , with files as {"name", "base64", "type"} objects ( "field+" appends, "field-" removes). pb_delete_collection , pb_truncate_collection , pb_delete_backup and pb_restore_backup need confirm set to the name. Endpoints that hand out a new token (auth-with- , auth-refresh, impersonate) and realtime (a stream) aren't tools. Each tool call counts against the API's rate limits, like any request. Batch sub-requests skip route middleware (PocketBase behaviour).

title: MCP
heading: Add your own tools from pb_hooks
text: Write the endpoint as you would anyway, then declare its tool at the top level of a hooks file: // pb_hooks/blog.pb.js routerAdd('POST', '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', (e) = { / … / }, $apis.requireSuperuserAuth()) $mcp.addEndpoint({ name: 'blog_publish_post', description: 'Publish a draft post and email subscribers.', method: 'POST', path: '/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish', // {id} comes from args.id inputSchema: { type: 'object', required: ['id'], properties: { id: { type: 'string' } } }, // optional; request is the default mapping, return a changed copy request: ({ args, auth, request }) = ({ ...request, body: { at: args.when } }), // optional; throw for an error the model can read response: ({ status, json }) = (status === 200 ? { published: json.id } : json), }) $mcp.instructions('blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.') The tool runs the request as the caller, so the route's own auth check is what protects it. One tool serves every caller. title , outputSchema and annotations are optional. Without annotations, GET tools are marked read-only and DELETE tools destructive. request gets {args, auth, request} and returns {method, path, query, body, headers, files} (missing keys keep the default; $mcp.pathValue(v) escapes a path segment). response gets {args, auth, status, headers, body, json, truncated} . Both run one at a time on the VM that loaded the hooks and may use the file's top-level variables; the REST call itself runs outside it. Keep them small: the work belongs in the endpoint. $mcp.tools() lists the registered tool names. Agents are told to prefer the app's own tools: when an app has any, the instructions sent on connect say to use them when one fits and fall back to pb_ , and the tool list shows them first. Put work that spans collections in a custom endpoint (one transaction, the app's checks), not in a chain of pb_ calls. A wrapper can sit over a stock endpoint too, to give it the app's meaning (for example notes_add_note over POST /api/collections/notes/records ).

title: MCP
heading: In the logs
text: Without OAuth Server on the app, MCP logs a warning on serve: mcp: ext/oauth-server isn't registered; /mcp accepts pasted PocketBase auth tokens only, and clients can't sign in by themselves . In pocketone it always is.

title: MCP
heading: Works with
text: OAuth Server Signs MCP clients in. MCP points clients at it from the protected resource metadata, turns on its client self-registration, and makes tokens bound to /mcp never expire. Who may sign in comes from its Collections (default: superusers and every auth collection). Tokens The access tokens are API tokens bound to https:// /mcp (RFC 8707): they work nowhere else, and are listed and revoked under Settings → API tokens. Your token scopes On a full-access connection a tool call holds every scope you registered (except ones its collection can't hold): $tokens.requireScope guards pass, and @request.headers.x_token_scope_ is "1" in collection rules. On a connection limited to scopes it holds only those, and requests they don't cover are refused (see Scopes). Pages A pb_pages +api.js route is a REST endpoint like any other; declare its tool with $mcp.addEndpoint . S3 Redirect pb_download_file follows its one redirect to storage. JS hooks $mcp in pb_hooks (above). Under Pocker, a Go build registers MCP (with Tokens and OAuth Server) in each instance's SetupApp ; there's no pluginkit plugin for it. The stock pocketone binary doesn't add it to pocker instances.

title: MCP
heading: Tools from Go
text: A plugin registered on the same app reaches the server with mcp.For(app) : server := mcp.For(app) // or the mcp.Server that mcp.MustRegister returned // the endpoint, as you'd write it anyway app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.POST("/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish", publish).Bind(apis.RequireSuperuserAuth()) return se.Next() }) // the tool wrapper server.MustAddEndpoint(mcp.Endpoint{ Name: "blog_publish_post", // lowercase _ _ ; pb_ is the built-ins' Title: "Publish post", Description: "Publish a draft post and email subscribers.", Method: http.MethodPost, Path: "/api/blog/posts/{id}/publish", // {id} is filled from args.id InputSchema: map[string]any{"type": "object", "required": []any{"id"}, "properties": map[string]any{"id": map[string]any{"type": "string"}}}, Annotations: mcp.Write, // default from the method: GET read-only, DELETE destructive Request: nil, // optional: func(c mcp.Call) ( mcp.Request, error) Response: nil, // optional: func(c mcp.Call, res mcp.Response) (any, error) }) server.AddInstructions("blog_publish_post also emails subscribers.") The default mapping: {name} path segments come from the argument of the same name, escaped. Empty, . and .. are refused (the router would clean them into another route). Other arguments go to the query string for GET , HEAD and DELETE , and to the JSON body for other methods. An argument holding a file, {"name": "a.png", "base64": "…", "type": "image/png"} or a list of them, makes the body multipart (other arguments ride along as @jsonPayload ), the way PocketBase takes uploads. Up to 10 MB per file. Arguments are checked against the schema's required , top-level type s, enum s and additionalProperties: false before the request is made; the endpoint validates the rest. The result: 2xx JSON comes back as the result (also as structuredContent when it's an object); other 2xx bodies as text; 4xx/5xx as a tool error with PocketBase's {status, message, data} , so the model can fix its call. JSON results are capped at 1 MB and say when they were cut. Request sees the caller ( c.Auth() ) but can't change who the request runs as: an Authorization header it sets is dropped. Build paths with c.Path(template) or mcp.PathValue , never by joining raw strings. c.Do makes another request as the same caller (e.g. a file token before a download). Response may return any JSON-able value, a string, or an mcp.Content list (images, text, embedded files). SuperuserOnly: true hides a tool from other callers' tool list.

title: MCP
heading: Tools from a plugin
text: A PocketOne plugin that adds tools names them _ _ : its name (with - as _ ), then at least two lowercase words, such as notes_list_notes or oauth_server_revoke_client . Each has a description, and an input schema, when it has one, is a JSON Schema object. The conformance test checks all of this when the plugin's test puts an MCP server on the test apps: conformance.Run(t, newPlugin, conformance.Options{Setup: func(app core.App) error { _, err := mcp.Register(app, mcp.Config{}) return err }})

title: MCP
heading: How sign-in works
text: With Tokens and OAuth Server on the app, /mcp uses OAuth the way Claude connectors and Claude Code expect: A request without a token gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https:// /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp" . The protected resource metadata names the app as its authorization server (OAuth Server's issuer). OAuth Server publishes the authorization server metadata, with PKCE S256, client metadata documents and dynamic registration. The client registers itself (Claude's published identity through a client metadata document, or dynamic registration), and the user signs in in a browser. The access token is an API token bound to https:// /mcp . It carries the account's rights but works only on /mcp . Each MCP request makes a PocketBase auth token for the same account, and tool calls reach the REST API with it (as Pages' ctx.pb() does). For a token limited to scopes, those requests carry the scopes ( tokens.WithScopes ), and Tokens checks them as it would a scoped token's request. Without OAuth Server, /mcp falls back to PocketBaseTokenAuth : pasted PocketBase auth tokens ( Collections limits which auth collections, default any), and the warning above. Config.Auth overrides the choice; mcp.OAuth{Issuer} overrides the authorization server listed in the metadata.

title: MCP
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with an MCP endpoint at /mcp : the built-in pb_ tools, a tool over a Go route and one over a JS route. cd example go run . serve The example registers devusers, so the logins are admin@example.com / password (superuser) and user@example.com / password (user). It also registers Tokens and OAuth Server for OAuth sign-in, and adds a tool over a Go route ( example_get_whoami ) and one over a JS route ( example_list_recent_users , in pb_hooks/mcp.pb.js ). Then: claude mcp add --transport http pb-example http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp claude mcp login pb-example // Command example runs one PocketBase app with an MCP endpoint at /mcp: the built-in pb_ tools (the whole stock REST // API), a tool over a Go route, and a tool over a JS route from pb_hooks/mcp.pb.js. // // cd ext/mcp/example && go run . serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. // // Sign-in is OAuth (ext/oauth-server + ext/tokens): add the endpoint to Claude Code and sign in in the browser when it // asks. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. // // claude mcp add --transport http pb-example http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp // claude mcp login pb-example (or /mcp in a session) package main import ( "log" "net/http" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/plugins/jsvm" "github.com/dop251/goja" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mcp" oauthserver "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/oauth-server" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // OAuth sign-in: API tokens + the authorization server. ext/mcp picks it up on serve and turns on dynamic client // registration. tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) oauthserver.MustRegister(app, oauthserver.Config{}) server := mcp.MustRegister(app, mcp.Config{ Name: "pb-example", Description: "Example PocketBase app with ext/mcp.", }) // A tool from Go: write the REST endpoint, then the tool wrapper. The tool runs the request as the caller, so // the route's own auth check is what protects it. app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/api/example/whoami", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"collection": e.Auth.Collection().Name, "email": e.Auth.Email()}) }).Bind(apis.RequireAuth()) return se.Next() }) server.MustAddEndpoint(mcp.Endpoint{ Name: "example_get_whoami", Title: "Who am I", Description: "The signed-in record's collection and email.", Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/api/example/whoami", }) jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ OnInit: func(vm goja.Runtime) { mcp.BindJS(vm, app) }, }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: MCP
heading: Go config
text: Path /mcp endpoint path Name , Version , Description , Icons app name slug, dev serverInfo Instructions generated first paragraph of the instructions sent on connect PublicURL the request's host origin used for the OAuth resource URL; set it when a proxy rewrites the host Auth OAuth{} with OAuth Server and Tokens, else PocketBaseTokenAuth{} the Authenticator BuiltinGroups all which pb_ groups ( mcp.BuiltinGroups ) ReadOnlyBuiltins false keep only the read-only pb_ tools NoBuiltins false drop every pb_ tool MaxResponse 1 MB cap on a JSON result MaxFile 10 MB cap on one file uploaded or downloaded through a tool AllowedOrigins none extra browser origins allowed besides the app's own The endpoint speaks MCP Streamable HTTP, stateless: each POST carries one JSON-RPC message and gets JSON back. Protocol versions 2025-11-25 , 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26 . Tools only for now.

title: Mothership
text: A control plane for a fleet of edges. The mothership is a PocketBase app that records which edges exist and which instances run where. Each edge follows it, serves its own instances and forwards requests for the rest to the edge that runs them. One operator, no users: owners and accounts are the tenants plugin (planned), which extends the mothership through its collections and the mirror's extensions. Each layer is optional: an edge runs without a mothership, and a mothership without tenants. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Mothership
heading: Install
text: The edge side (the mirror package) is built into pocketone . It turns on when pocketone.yaml names a provider and has a mothership section (below); pocketone serve then takes its instances and the other edges from the mothership. The mothership side has no switch yet. In the Go code of the PocketBase app that will be the mothership, create its collections once the app has bootstrapped: if err := mothership.EnsureCollections(app); err != nil { return err } The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mothership . In your own edge build, mirror.FromSection(log) returns the mirror for the config (nil without a mothership section); use it as the host's instance source and the router's edge source, as examples/pocketone/multi.go does.

title: Mothership
heading: Configure
text: On each edge, add a mothership section next to the provider. Logins come from the private .env : provider: docker # or pocker mothership: url: http://10.88.0.10:8090 email: $MOTHERSHIP_EMAIL password: $MOTHERSHIP_PASSWORD self: lax-1 # this edge's edge_id (or edges.self) internal_url: http://10.88.0.5:8080 region: lax apex: example.com # .example.com routes to each instance url and self are required. The edge logs in as a superuser of the mothership. On the mothership, there's nothing to configure beyond creating the collections.

title: Mothership
heading: mothership:
text: A community mothership to mirror instances and edges from: url, login, this edge's id, internal URL, region, apex. url string The mothership's URL. Required. email string Superuser email this edge logs in with; use a $VAR from the .env. password string Superuser password; use a $VAR from the .env. self string This edge's edge_id, such as lax-1. Default: the edges section's self. Required. internal_url string Where other edges reach this one. Set: the edge registers itself when the mothership has no record for it. region string Region recorded when the edge registers itself. apex string Makes . a hostname of every instance. Empty: hosts only. heartbeat duration How often this edge marks itself online. Default 15s; negative: never. resync duration How often everything is reloaded, in case a change was missed. Default 10m.

title: Mothership
heading: Use
text: You manage the fleet in the mothership's dashboard, in two collections only superusers can read or write: edges : edge_id (such as lax-1 ), internal_url , region , status ( online , draining , offline ) and last_seen . An edge with internal_url set registers itself when it has no record, marks itself online every 15 s, and offline when it shuts down. instances : name ( . routes to it), hosts (extra hostnames), edge (where it runs), power (off answers 409 "instance is powered off"), suspension (non-empty answers 403 with that message), dev , version , secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , plugins and status . Changes reach the edges within moments over PocketBase's realtime stream; there's no polling. To move an instance, change its edge : the old edge drops its full record and forwards to the new one until the new edge has it. An instance with no edge isn't served anywhere.

title: Mothership
heading: Works with
text: Host The mirror is the host's instance source: which instances exist and which this edge runs. Edge The mirror is also an edge source: where the other edges are, so requests for their instances are forwarded. It combines with a fixed edges list. Docker and Pocker Run the instances this edge owns, with the version, secrets, limits and plugin settings from each record. Tenants (planned) Adds owners and accounts through mirror extensions.

title: Mothership
heading: Building on Mothership
text: Your own fields and collections. EnsureCollections leaves fields an extension added alone, so a plugin can add its own fields and collections to the mothership. Mirror extensions. Pass a mirror.Extension to mirror.FromSection or mirror.Config.Extensions . Views() adds filtered subscriptions (such as owners filtered to instances_via_owner.edge ?= {edge} ), Instance() adjusts each instance as it's built (block a suspended owner's instances, add an owner's trusted IPs), and Changed() names the instances a change in its views affects. Go API. mirror.New(mirror.Config{...}) builds a mirror without the config file. Get(view, id) and Records(view) read any view; SelfRecord() is this edge's record id.

title: Mothership
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. The stock binary's multi-instance mode, examples/pocketone/multi.go , follows a mothership when the config has the section.

title: Mothership
heading: How it works
text: Each edge subscribes to filtered views, so it only receives what concerns it: edges edges all forwarding, and health from heartbeats routes instances fields id,name,hosts,edge,updated the routing table: any edge may get any visitor local instances edge = full records (secrets, limits, plugins) for instances this edge runs An instance moving away shows up in routes and its full record is dropped; one moving here arrives in local . The stream reconnects and reloads on its own, and reloads everything every 10 minutes in case anything was missed. Filters cut what each edge downloads and keeps (most edges run a few of thousands of instances). They are not a security boundary while edges log in as superusers.

title: Mothership
heading: Status
text: Early. Built: the edges and instances collections ( EnsureCollections ) and the edge side ( mirror ). Not yet: the mothership's own endpoints (placement, moves) and instance status reports.

title: OAuth Server
text: Makes your app an OAuth 2.1 authorization server whose access tokens are API tokens. pocketone login signs in to it in the browser (or with a code on another device), and MCP clients such as Claude or ChatGPT connectors register themselves and connect. Superusers and app users sign in on your app's own pages, through PocketBase's own auth endpoints. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: OAuth Server
heading: Install
text: OAuth Server is built into pocketone and always on, with Tokens. There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, register Tokens and OAuth Server before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) // required: access tokens are API tokens remotes.MustRegister(app, remotes.Config{}) // optional: lists "oauth" in /_pocker/whoami so login finds it oauthserver.MustRegister(app, oauthserver.Config{}) app.Start() Without Tokens the app refuses to start ("oauth-server needs ext/tokens"). The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/oauth-server .

title: OAuth Server
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for OAuth Server. In pocketone : superusers and every auth collection may sign in; access tokens last 30 days, refresh tokens 180 days (renewed on each refresh); tokens for MCP never expire, since MCP turns that on for /mcp ; client self-registration ( POST /oauth/register ) is on, since MCP turns it on; Claude and Claude Code connect without registering (their client metadata documents from claude.ai and claude.com are trusted). A Go build can change these (see Go config).

title: OAuth Server
heading: Sign-in methods
text: The pages offer exactly the methods each auth collection has on, so you set them where you always do: the collection's options in the dashboard ( Collections → the collection → Options ). Password , One-time password (an emailed code) and OAuth2 providers each get their own form or button. Multi-factor authentication adds a second step. The collection's auth rule (for example verified = true ) applies. OAuth2 providers (Google, GitHub, …) are offered to app users only; PocketBase doesn't allow them for superusers. Register /oauth/provider/callback as a redirect URI with each provider. The pages show Settings → Application → Application name .

title: OAuth Server
heading: Behind a proxy
text: The server names itself (the issuer) after the scheme and host the browser used, with https when the request is TLS or X-Forwarded-Proto says so. If a proxy rewrites the host, set Config.Issuer in a Go build so the issuer and the provider callback URL stay stable.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Scopes
text: A client may ask for any scope registered with Tokens, including your own from $tokens.registerScope . offline_access is accepted (refresh tokens are always issued). The consent page lets the user decide: Full access (no scopes: the account's full rights) or Only these , with a box for each scope. The scopes the client asked for start ticked; the others the account may hold are there to tick, except ones that only reach /_pocker/ routes (like deploy ), which appear only when asked for. With no scopes asked, Full access starts selected. The token gets exactly what was ticked, and the token response's scope says which.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Your own sign-in pages
text: The built-in pages (sign-in, second step, one-time code, consent, device code, done, error) follow the system's light or dark mode and work on phones. To change them, eject them as PocketPages templates: pocketone oauth eject # --force overwrites files you already have It writes signin.ejs , mfa.ejs , otp.ejs , consent.ejs , device.ejs , done.ejs , error.ejs and the shared head.ejs , foot.ejs and hidden.ejs (with the CSS) to pb_pages/_private/oauth/ , and prints each file. From then on the server renders your templates; a missing one falls back to the built-in page, so delete them to go back. _private keeps them from being served as routes. See Custom page templates for the data they get.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Signing in
text: Whenever a client sends someone to your app ( pocketone login , Claude, an app of yours), they see: Sign in to : the form for app users ( users first; with several user collections, a tab for each). At the bottom, Sign in as a superuser switches to the superuser form, which looks clearly different: a Superuser badge, Superuser sign-in , its own colors and a warning. Sign in as a user instead goes back. One more step when the account has MFA, offering its other methods. After a password, when an emailed code is the only method left, it's sent right away. Check your email for an emailed code. The consent page: the client's name, the account, whether the client will act as a user (and which collection) or as a superuser, and the access: Full access or Only these scopes (see Scopes). Click Allow or Deny , or Not ? Use another account . With no user collection allowed, the superuser form is the only one. A browser stays signed in to these pages for 15 minutes. Failed attempts are limited to 10 per IP in 5 minutes. On another device (over SSH, say), the client shows a code like WDJB-MJHT . Open https:// /oauth/device/verify , enter it under Connect a device , sign in and allow. Codes last 10 minutes.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Log in from the command line
text: pocketone login prod With OAuth Server on the remote, Remotes opens your browser on the pages above, or shows a device code when there's no browser ( --device asks for one). The client is the built-in pocketbase-cli , named pocketone CLI on the consent page (the name follows the command, so another build shows its own).

title: OAuth Server
heading: See and revoke what's connected
text: Every sign-in creates an API token named " (OAuth)". They're listed under Settings → API tokens with an oauth: label; click Revoke to disconnect a client. Revoking the access token also ends its refresh token. A client can revoke its own tokens at POST /oauth/revoke , which pocketone logout does.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Register clients
text: Claude and the CLI need no registration, and MCP clients register themselves. For your own app: pocketone oauth clients add --name "My app" --redirect https://myapp.example.com/callback pocketone oauth clients add --name "Desktop" --redirect http://127.0.0.1/callback --public pocketone oauth clients list pocketone oauth clients rm add prints the client id, and the secret once for a confidential client. --public makes a client with no secret (PKCE only), for desktop and mobile apps. --redirect can be repeated. Redirect URIs must be https , http on a loopback address, or an app's custom scheme. Loopback URIs match any port (RFC 8252); others must match exactly.

title: OAuth Server
heading: In the logs
text: oauth-server: this collection may sign in but can't own API tokens; add it to tokens.Config.Collections , once per collection, when Tokens is narrowed in a Go build. The page then says signing in with that account type "isn't set up on this server yet". oauth-server: auth methods (error) when a collection's sign-in methods can't be read. oauth-server: cleanup (warning) when the half-hourly removal of expired codes fails.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Works with
text: Tokens Required. Access tokens are API tokens owned by whoever signed in, with the client's id, the granted scopes and the audience. Every scope registered with Tokens can be requested. Remotes OAuth Server lists itself as the oauth feature in /_pocker/whoami ; pocketone login then signs in in the browser (loopback redirect with PKCE) or with a device code, and renews through the refresh token. MCP MCP points clients here from its protected resource metadata, turns on self-registration, and makes tokens bound to /mcp never expire. Tool calls run as whoever signed in. Deploy pocketone login gives the deploy commands a token for the account that signed in. Pages pocketone oauth eject writes the pages as PocketPages templates, rendered from then on. Under Pocker, a Go build registers OAuth Server (and Tokens) in each instance's SetupApp ; there's no pluginkit plugin for it yet. The stock pocketone binary doesn't add it to pocker instances.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Audience (RFC 8707)
text: A resource parameter on /oauth/authorize , /oauth/device or /oauth/token (a URL on this server) binds the access token to it: the token then only works under that URL's path. So a token issued for /mcp can't deploy, and a deploy token can't drive MCP. Refreshed tokens keep it.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Building on OAuth Server
text: Go API. oauthserver.For(app) returns the server. Issuer(e) is its public base URL; EnableDynamicRegistration() turns on POST /oauth/register ; SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) sets the lifetime of tokens bound to a resource (0: never expire). FindClient , ListClients , AddClient and RemoveClient manage clients. Scopes. Register a scope with Tokens (Go or $tokens.registerScope ) and clients can ask for it; nothing else is needed. Render the pages yourself. Config.Render(e, page, data) renders any page (return handled=false to fall back), with PageData . It wins over ejected templates.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Example
text: go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 go run ./example login http://127.0.0.1:8090 # opens the browser; --device for a code example/main.go , below, registers Tokens, Remotes and OAuth Server with self-registration on and some branding. Logins from devusers: user@example.com / password on the default form, admin@example.com / password after Sign in as a superuser . // Command example is a PocketBase that is an OAuth server: pocketbase login signs in to it in the browser, and MCP // clients can register themselves (dynamic registration is on here). // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 // go run ./example login http://127.0.0.1:8090 # opens the browser; --device for a code // go run ./example remote whoami http://127.0.0.1:8090 // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): app user user@example.com / password (the default form), superuser // admin@example.com / password ("Sign in as a superuser"). package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" oauthserver "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/oauth-server" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/remotes" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" // OAuth access tokens are API tokens, owned by whoever signed in: superusers and app users tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) // any auth record may own tokens (the default) remotes.MustRegister(app, remotes.Config{}) // whoami discovery + login/remote commands oauthserver.MustRegister(app, oauthserver.Config{ DynamicRegistration: true, // MCP connectors register themselves Branding: oauthserver.Branding{Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Example OAuth server"}, }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: OAuth Server
heading: Endpoints
text: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server Metadata (RFC 8414). The issuer is Config.Issuer , else the request's own scheme and host. GET/POST /oauth/authorize Sign-in and consent pages. Authorization code with PKCE (S256 only; required). POST /oauth/token authorization_code , refresh_token and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code . Refresh rotates without logouts: the old access token lives out its time, and the old refresh token works again for 2 minutes, so two processes refreshing at once both succeed. POST /oauth/device , GET/POST /oauth/device/verify Device flow (RFC 8628): codes like WDJB-MJHT , valid 10 minutes. POST /oauth/revoke Revocation (RFC 7009): an access token or a refresh token (revokes both). GET/POST /oauth/provider/callback Where OAuth2 providers send the browser back after sign-in. POST /oauth/register Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591), when DynamicRegistration is on or a plugin called EnableDynamicRegistration() (MCP does). Public clients by default. Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) belongs to the resource: MCP serves /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource .

title: OAuth Server
heading: Clients
text: pocketbase-cli is built in: public, any http://127.0.0.1: /… or [::1] redirect, device codes. It's what pocketone login uses. Client ID metadata documents (CIMD): an https:// client id is fetched as a JSON document ( client_id must equal the URL; its client_name and redirect_uris are used; public clients only; cached 10 minutes). Only Config.CIMDHosts are trusted (default claude.ai , claude.com ); the metadata says client_id_metadata_document_supported . Registered clients live in _oauth_clients ; codes, device codes and refresh tokens in _oauth_codes .

title: OAuth Server
heading: How sign-in works
text: The pages never check passwords or codes themselves. Each step calls PocketBase's own auth endpoint in-process, through the app's router, so the collection's auth rule, MFA, rate limits, superuser IP limits and every onRecordAuth Request hook apply as for the REST API, and the record the endpoint returns is the one signed in: password: POST /api/collections/{c}/auth-with-password ; emailed code: POST …/request-otp , then POST …/auth-with-otp ; OAuth2: the browser goes to the provider with the state and PKCE from GET …/auth-methods , comes back to /oauth/provider/callback , and POST …/auth-with-oauth2 completes it (account linking and sign-up are PocketBase's); MFA: when an auth call answers 401 with an mfaId , the second page passes it along. Only collections with a sign-in method on are offered. Access tokens are owned by the signed-in record, so every collection that may sign in must also be allowed by Tokens (its default is every auth collection). The session is a 15-minute HttpOnly cookie on /oauth ; forms carry a CSRF token; a provider round trip keeps its state in a signed 10-minute cookie.

title: OAuth Server
heading: Go config
text: oauthserver.MustRegister(app, oauthserver.Config{ Collections: nil, // who may sign in; default: _superusers + every auth collection AccessTTL: 30 24 time.Hour, // default; per resource with srv.SetAccessTTL("/mcp", 0) RefreshTTL: 180 24 time.Hour, // default, renewed on each refresh DynamicRegistration: false, // POST /oauth/register (MCP turns it on) CIMDHosts: nil, // default claude.ai, claude.com; an empty non-nil slice turns CIMD off Issuer: "", // public base URL; default: the request's scheme and host Branding: oauthserver.Branding{LogoURL: "/logo.svg", Accent: "#4f46e5", Footer: "Acme Inc."}, }) Branding also takes a Name (default: Settings → Application name). Accent is the button color (default #16161a ).

title: OAuth Server
heading: Custom page templates
text: Ejected templates get ctx.data : PageData in camelCase ( data.appName , data.action , data.hidden , data.csrf , data.clientName , data.scopes , data.scopeChoices , data.superuser , data.providers , data.error , …). Every POST form must include include('/oauth/hidden') and a step button. Steps: password , request_otp , otp , oauth2: , use: (switch forms; use: is the default user form), allow , deny , switch . Sign-in forms post collection ; the MFA and code pages also post mfa_id / otp_id . Consent posts access = full , or limited with a grant field per ticked scope (from data.scopeChoices : name , description , checked ). A consent form without access grants what the client asked for.
