title: Pocker
text: Pocker hosts many PocketBase instances in one process. It is PocketBase itself (this repo tracks upstream PocketBase and shares its history) plus a small engine in this folder, run by the stock pocketone binary as a runtime provider ( provider: pocker in pocketone.yaml). One port, many instances. Each request's hostname maps to a canonical instance id. Each instance is a normal PocketBase folder, / ( pb_data , pb_hooks , pb_migrations , pb_public ), with its own environment for JS hooks ( $os.getenv , process.env ), its own JS migrations and its own settings encryption key. An instance's app starts on its first request (tens of milliseconds) and keeps running.

title: Pocker
heading: Dev mode: any hostname
text: # pocketone.yaml server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" } provider: pocker instances: { dev: true } pocker: { root: ./pb_root } pocketone serve curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost A hostname the instance source doesn't map uses the hostname itself as its id (lowercase, no port, no trailing dot; anything that isn't a safe folder name gets 400), its folder is created on first use, and apps run in PocketBase dev mode. The instances file (or another source) is optional in dev mode; hosts it maps keep their own ids.

title: Pocker
heading: Production: mapped hostnames only
text: Without dev mode, Pocker serves only what an instance source maps. The built-in source is the instances section's YAML file (reloaded when it changes; the host refuses to start without it): # instances.yaml instances: id: blog # folder /blog hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com] id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... } # the app's environment encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef # encrypts PocketBase's stored settings; not visible to JS access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] } plugins: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } } # settings for plugins, by name id: old hosts: [old.example.com] blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" } Unknown hosts get 404 and no folder is ever created from a request. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes. Hosting platforms plug in their own InstanceSource (for example a control plane streaming the hostname - id map over SSE) instead of the file; a community mothership is one (the mothership section, ext/mothership). pocketone.yaml for a production host (each plugin owns its section; every field has a default): server: https: ":443" http: ":80" # redirects to HTTPS (and answers ACME HTTP-01 challenges) plain: [] # extra plain-HTTP listeners (no TLS, no redirect), e.g. a private network other servers forward on tls: { cert: /path/fullchain.pem, key: /path/privkey.pem } # re-read when they change; or the autotls section provider: pocker instances: { file: ./instances.yaml } pocker: root: ./pb_root hooks_pool_size: 2 egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach (default none) # default limits for every instance (each instance can override them, see below) max_js_execution: 30s # any single JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) max_js_allocation: 64MiB # one-shot JS allocations max_call_stack_size: 2000 max_sleep: 10s max_query_duration: 30s # any SQL statement without its own deadline http_send_max_timeout: 60s http_send_max_body: 10MiB max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail rate_limits: # per client IP and per instance; trusted clients get the trusted set ip_hourly: 1000 instance_hourly: 10000 ip_concurrent: 15 instance_concurrent: 250 file_weight: 0.1 # a /api/files request costs a tenth trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 } # off: true # no rate limiting (the default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set) firewall: allow_cidrs: [] # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone); others get 403 trusted_proxies: [] # peers whose client-IP headers are believed client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP] trusted_clients: [] # client IPs with the trusted limits on every instance trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP] # a trusted client names its end user (own buckets) rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit # autotls: # automatic certificates (ACME, via CertMagic, Caddy's certificate engine) # auto: true # email: ops@example.com # ca: letsencrypt # letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL # storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs # domains: [" .example.com", "example.com"] # obtained up front; wildcards need dns # dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN } # only needed for wildcards Firewall (ext/firewall; on whenever the config has firewall or rate_limits ). Peers outside allow_cidrs get 403. The client IP comes from client_ip_headers only when the peer is a trusted proxy, otherwise it is the peer. Rate-limited requests get 429 with Retry-After and a message naming the limit; every routed response carries -{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining} and -{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset , listed in Access-Control-Expose-Headers . Long-lived responses (realtime) hold their concurrency slot until they end. TLS. Certificate files are core ( server.tls ). Automatic certificates are ext/autotls (its autotls section): with auto: true and no dns , every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on its first TLS handshake (HTTP-01 / TLS-ALPN-01), with any DNS host and no API token; hostnames no instance serves never trigger issuance. A DNS provider (Cloudflare for now) is only needed for wildcard domains , proved through DNS-01; a wildcard without one is a config error. Each instance can override any of those limits (zero or missing fields keep the default): instances: id: shop hosts: [shop.example.com] limits: max_js_execution: 60s max_js_allocation: 128MiB id: api hosts: [api.example.com] access: { cors_origins: [https://app.example.com] } limits: { max_concurrent_js: 32 } plugins: firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }

title: Pocker
heading: Plugins
text: pocker.Provider.Plugins (or pocker.Server.Plugins in Go) takes plugins (see plugin.go ). Each implements Name() and any of: pluginkit.Plugin a PocketOne plugin, registered on every instance's app before it bootstraps ( Register(app, cfg) ) with the instance's plugins. settings, its id in pluginkit.AppID(app) ; e.g. pitr, storage, tokens, s3redirect, mailrelay, bulkmail. enabled: false skips it for that instance. A change to an instance's plugins: settings restarts its app on its next request. The same value works on a single app. Configurer reading its own pocketone.yaml section before the server starts ( Configure(cfg) ) Gate a peer check before routing, and admission (e.g. rate limits) before an instance is served or forwarded TLSProvider the main listener's TLS (e.g. automatic certificates) Wrapper wrapping the server's handler (the first listed is outermost) Starter background work once the Manager exists AppIniter host code that needs the whole Instance when setting up its app ( InitApp(inst, app) ); runs on every start, including restarts. Plugins use pluginkit.Plugin instead, so they run on a single app too and pass the conformance test. Per-instance settings for a plugin go under the instance's plugins. (read them with pocker.DecodePluginConfig ). app.Restart() (PocketBase's backup restore, pitr) restarts only that instance, not the process. Timings for the Server-Timing header are registered with pocker.Timing(ctx, fn) . The stock pocketone binary runs pocker with servertiming, autotls and mailtrap; the firewall turns on from its sections.

title: Pocker
heading: Platform values and logs
text: Superusers ( superusers: [{email, password_hash, id?, token_key?}] ) are upserted into the app's _superusers in Go when it starts, e.g. so a hosting platform's login works in the dashboard. Nothing goes through env. Private values ( private: {...} ) are for the host application's Go code and never visible to JS. A host registers that code with Server.SetupApp(inst, app) , which runs after migrations and before the app serves (for example a backup route checked against inst.Private["backup_token"] ). Secrets ( secrets: {...} ) are the instance's environment: what its JS sees through $os.getenv / process.env , and nothing else. No names are reserved; platform settings are explicit fields. Encryption key ( encryption_key ) encrypts PocketBase's stored settings (like --encryptionEnv ). JS never sees it. Access ( access: {cors_origins} ) is the owner's say over which browser origins may call the instance (PocketBase matching: exact, , wildcards; empty = any). Client IPs that get the trusted rate limits are the firewall's plugins.firewall.trusted_ips (on top of the process-wide firewall.trusted_clients ). Plugins ( plugins: { : ...} ) are per-instance settings for plugins; plugins read them once, so changing them restarts the app on its next request. Logs: PocketBase's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance in its pb_data . console. from JS hooks goes to /logs/exec.log as JSON lines {message, stream, time} ( stdout for log/info/debug, stderr for warn/error), rotated to exec.log.1 at 10 MiB. A start failure (e.g. a broken hooks file) is written there too, and only that instance fails. When an instance's secrets , encryption_key , access , limits , dev , dir , superusers , private or remote changes, its app restarts on the next request (the old one finishes in-flight requests first), so a rotated secret takes effect immediately. Host changes apply without a restart. GET /_pocker/health on any host reports {status, instances, running} . Changing an instance's files from host code (deploys, restores): Manager.WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn) stops the app, holds new requests for that instance, runs fn(dir) , then lets them through to a fresh app. Manager.StartInstance(ctx, id) starts it right away and returns the start error (for example to tell a deploy that a hook is broken), Manager.Running(id) says whether it is started, and Manager.InstanceDir(id) gives its folder. Manager.Ready() says whether the instance list has loaded. Manager.LogInstance(id, stream, message) appends to the instance's logs/exec.log (e.g. a scheduled job's result). Host code that runs in its own goroutines gets the Manager from Server.OnStart , before any request is served. Several servers, one set of instances. An instance with remote: runs on another server: Pocker checks the peer and the instance's rate limits here, then forwards the request (a reverse proxy to the URL by default; Server.Forward replaces it, e.g. to hold requests while the other server restarts). Its app never starts here, and an app already running here stops when remote is set. plain_listen gives the other servers a plain-HTTP port on a private network, and Manager.Firewall() lets host routes in front of the Manager use the same peer check.

title: Pocker
heading: Sandbox
text: Every instance's JS hooks and migrations run in a sandbox (the sandbox plugin), and its SQL runs behind SQLite's authorizer ( sandbox/sqlguard.go ). The sandbox plugin also owns the egress policy ( sandbox/egress.go ); pocker turns it on for its instances. sandbox_test.go runs one attack per route from one instance against another instance and the host; all of these are refused: Files: $os. , $filepath.glob/walk , $filesystem.fileFromPath , $template.loadFiles , $apis.static , require() Confined to the instance folder with an os.Root : the kernel resolves every path beneath it, refusing .. and symlinks that leave it. Relative paths and absolute paths inside the folder ( __hooks + "/x" ) work as before. Host primitives: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args , $filesystem.local Disabled ( $os.args is empty). Environment: $os.getenv , process.env Only the instance's own secrets . Go internals: $app.restart/bootstrap/runAllMigrations/onServe/onTerminate/onBootstrap/cron/unsafeWithoutHooks , hook.bindFunc/bind/trigger/unbind , sql.DB/Conn/Tx/Stmt (e.g. dbx.DB.DB() ), database/sql/driver , os/exec , net , syscall , http.Server controls Hidden from JS (the field-name mapper maps them to nothing). Top-level onRecord , routerAdd , cronAdd and the rest of $app work as usual. Raw SQL ( $app.db().newQuery ) Allowed. SQLite's authorizer refuses ATTACH (and VACUUM INTO ) outside the instance's pb_data , PRAGMA temp_store_directory/data_store_directory and load_extension ; the CLI-only readfile / writefile / fsdir don't exist in the library. Statements without a deadline get max_query_duration . CPU Every JS call is interrupted after max_js_execution ; sleep() is capped at 10 s. Memory, one shot Built-ins that allocate a large result in one step refuse results over max_js_allocation : String.repeat/padStart/padEnd , Array.join/toString , ArrayBuffer , typed arrays (incl. array-likes, .from , and reaching the constructor through an instance), Buffer.alloc / new Buffer , $os.readFile , fileFromPath , readerToString / toBytes limits. Recursion depth is capped (a JS stack overflow would otherwise crash the Go process). Memory, gradual Not limited. goja has no per-VM memory accounting, so a hook's gradual growth counts against the whole process; the process can use the host's swap, and the OS is the last line. (A memory watch with strikes and quarantine was removed on 2026-11-14: it could fail requests where swap would have absorbed them, and it never fired in production.) Outbound network: $http.send , $filesystem.fileFromURL , S3 storage and backups, OAuth2/JWK fetches, SMTP Public addresses only, checked on the address actually connected to (after DNS, so rebinding doesn't help): loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata, CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges, and IPv6 equivalents/IPv4-in-IPv6 are refused unless listed in egress_allow . Installed process-wide on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client ( pocker/egress.go ). Host code that must reach private addresses (e.g. a control plane over a private network) uses its own http.Client with its own transport. $http.send timeouts and response bodies are capped. Limits of the memory controls: only one-shot allocations are capped. A hook that grows memory gradually slows or, past swap, restarts the whole process (every instance in it) rather than failing alone; per-instance memory accounting needs a goja with a memory API, or one process per instance (the docker provider). Not covered yet: per-instance concurrency limits, and OS-level defence in depth: run Pocker as a non-root user with an OS firewall that only lets that user reach public addresses (a second, independent egress layer), plus seccomp and Landlock.

title: Pocker
heading: Changes to PocketBase
text: These live in the repo root (PocketBase's own files), not in this plugin. Kept small and marked // PocketOne: so upstream merges stay easy: core.BaseAppConfig.AppMigrations : a per-app migrations list (JS migrations from plugins/jsvm register there instead of the global core.AppMigrations ). core.BaseAppConfig.EncryptionKey : the settings encryption key passed in directly instead of read from the process environment. plugins/jsvm : Config.Extensions ( extension.go ): values with optional methods ( OnInit , OnCall around every call into JS, HTTPClient for $http.send , HookFiles / MigrationFiles / Require , OnLoad / OnCompile for error mapping), plus Run and ScriptPath . The sandbox, jsembed and jserrors are extensions. Mail needs no core change: the sandbox sends an app's own SMTP through the egress policy on OnMailerSend ( sandbox.BindMail ).

title: Pocker
heading: Versions
text: PocketOne has its own version line, starting at v0.0.1 , independent of PocketBase's numbers. When PocketBase releases, we merge it and decide then how to bump ours. Each release says which PocketBase version it's based on. The module path stays ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase , so a build pins a PocketOne version through the replace line: replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase = github.com/pockethost/pocketone v0.0.1

title: Pocker
heading: Upstream tracking
text: Fetch upstream without its tags: PocketBase's v0.x tags must never land in this repo, or Go would take v0.41.1 for the newest PocketOne. git remote add upstream https://ganigeorgiev.com/git/pocketbase/pocketbase git config remote.upstream.tagOpt --no-tags git fetch upstream refs/tags/v0.41.2 # one release, without creating the tag here git merge FETCH_HEAD # resolve conflicts in the PocketOne-marked spots, rerun go test ./core/... ./plugins/jsvm/... and go test ./... in ext/pocker and ext/sandbox

title: Remotes
text: Named remotes for the pocketone command: the apps a project deploys to, each signed in to once. Give an app a name like prod , log in, and commands such as pocketone deploy prod know where to go and who you are. pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com pocketone login prod pocketone deploy prod # Deploy Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Remotes
heading: Install
text: Remotes is built into pocketone and on : the remote , login , logout and link commands are always there, and every app it serves answers GET /_pocker/whoami so other machines can sign in to it. There's nothing to install. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() remotes.MustRegister(app, remotes.Config{}) // whoami route; on pocketbase.PocketBase also the commands app.Start() The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/remotes . Add Tokens so a password login can create a revocable API token, and OAuth Server for browser login.

title: Remotes
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen. Remotes keeps two files and reads a few environment variables.

title: Remotes
heading: The project's remotes
text: .pocketbase/remotes.json in the project holds names and URLs only, so commit it: {"default": "prod", "remotes": {"prod": {"url": "https://myapp.example.com"}}} Commands find it by walking up from the current folder. It isn't a pb_ name, since pb_ folders are deployed. A project linked with npx pockethost link has a .pockethostconfig ( {"instanceName": "myapp"} ). It reads as the remote pockethost → https://myapp.pockethost.io (a name with a dot is taken as a custom domain).

title: Remotes
heading: Saved logins
text: Logins are saved per user, keyed by URL, in ~/.config/pocketone/credentials.json (mode 0600). Set POCKETONE_CONFIG_DIR to use another folder; with XDG_CONFIG_HOME set, it's $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pocketone/ .

title: Remotes
heading: Environment variables
text: POCKETONE_TOKEN_ A token for one remote, for CI. The name is upper case, other characters as _ ( POCKETONE_TOKEN_PROD ). POCKETONE_TOKEN A token for any remote. POCKETHOST_TOKEN A token for the pockethost remote. POCKETONE_PASSWORD The password for login --email , so it isn't asked for. A token in the environment wins over a saved login. The POCKETONE in these names and the pocketone folder come from the command's name, so a build shipped under another name uses its own ( POCKETHOST_TOKEN , ~/.config/pockethost ).

title: Remotes
heading: Manage remotes
text: pocketone remote add prod https://myapp.example.com --default pocketone remote list # names, URLs and who you're logged in as; marks the default pocketone remote default prod pocketone remote rm staging # the saved login stays; see logout pocketone remote whoami prod # who you are there, your token's scopes, and what the app offers A URL without a scheme gets https:// . The first remote you add becomes the default. A command that names no remote uses the default, else the only remote, else the one called default . Any command also takes a URL in place of a name: pocketone deploy https://other.example.com .

title: Remotes
heading: Log in
text: pocketone login prod login tries, in order: The browser , when the remote runs OAuth Server. Your browser opens, you sign in and approve, and the command finishes. Over SSH or without a display it shows a code to enter on another device instead; --device asks for that, and --no-browser prints the URL without opening it. A pasted token ( pbt_... , a PocketHost token, or a PocketBase auth token). At the prompt, paste it, or pass --token or --token-stdin . Email and password. Type a superuser email at the prompt, or pass --email (or --password to skip the browser). --collection picks another auth collection (default _superusers ). If the account has MFA, a one-time code is sent and asked for. A password login creates an API token named "pocketone CLI on " and saves that, never the session, so the remote needs Tokens. A browser login keeps a refresh token and renews itself when it's within a day of expiring. You'll see Logged in to https://myapp.example.com as admin@example.com (oauth).

title: Remotes
heading: Link in one step
text: pocketone link https://myapp.example.com pocketone link https://myapp.pockethost.io ph_pat_... link adds the remote (named default , or --name ), makes it the default if there's none yet, and logs in. It takes the same login flags.

title: Remotes
heading: Log out
text: pocketone logout prod Forgets the saved login. It also revokes it on the remote: the API token a password login created, or the browser login's refresh token. If the remote can't be reached, it tells you to revoke it in the dashboard.

title: Remotes
heading: Works with
text: Deploy deploy , dev , pull and logs resolve their remote and login through Remotes, and find the deploy API through /_pocker/whoami . OAuth Server Advertises itself as the oauth feature in /_pocker/whoami ; login then signs in through the browser (loopback redirect on 127.0.0.1 with PKCE) or a device code. Tokens Password logins create an API token, and logout deletes it. Whoami reports a token's id and scopes. PocketHost .pockethostconfig and POCKETHOST_TOKEN work as the pockethost remote. A remote without /_pocker/whoami takes a pasted token as is.

title: Remotes
heading: GET /_pocker/whoami
text: Every app with Remotes answers who the request's credential is and what the app offers, so clients can discover features: {"auth": {"collection": "_superusers", "id": "…", "email": "admin@example.com"}, "via": "token", "tokenId": "…", "scopes": ["deploy"], "features": {"deploy": "/_pocker/deploy/v1", "tokens": "/api/tokens"}, "app": {"name": "Acme", "url": "https://myapp.example.com"}} via is token for an API token, jwt for a PocketBase auth token, and empty with no credential ( auth is then null ). Every API token may call it, whatever its scopes.

title: Remotes
heading: Building on Remotes
text: Advertise a feature. remotes.Advertise(app, "deploy", "/_pocker/deploy/v1") lists it in whoami. Deploy and OAuth Server do this; Tokens is detected without importing it. Go client. remotes.Open(dir, name) resolves a remote and its credential (environment first, then the saved login, renewing a browser login when due) and returns a remotes.Client : base URL, bearer token, an HTTP client with short connect timeouts, and JSON , NewRequest , Do and Whoami . Deploy's commands build on it. Commands. remotes.Commands() returns the remote , login , logout and link commands, for a binary that isn't a pocketbase.PocketBase . Login. remotes.BrowserLogin is the hook login tries first; this package fills it with its OAuth client.

title: Remotes
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is an app with remotes and API tokens. Run two copies and add one as a remote of the other; its comment has the commands. // Command example is a PocketBase with remotes and API tokens: run two copies, add one as a remote of the other's // project and sign in. // // go run ./example serve --http=127.0.0.1:8090 # the "remote" // go run ./example remote add local http://127.0.0.1:8090 # in a project folder // go run ./example login local --email admin@example.com # password: password; mints a pbt_ token // go run ./example remote whoami // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/remotes" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) // so login can mint a revocable API token remotes.MustRegister(app, remotes.Config{}) // GET /_pocker/whoami + remote/login/logout/link commands if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Redirect
text: File downloads as short-lived signed redirects to your bucket, after PocketBase's own access check. When an app keeps its files in S3 (Settings → Files storage), PocketBase normally downloads each file from the bucket and streams it to the browser. With S3 Redirect, /api/files/... answers 302 with a presigned GET URL instead, and the browser fetches the file straight from the bucket. The app's bandwidth, memory and connections stay free. With Cloudflare R2 the downloads cost no egress either. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Install
text: S3 Redirect is built into pocketone and on by default . It only acts when S3 file storage is on: turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage and downloads redirect. With files on local disk, nothing changes. To stream files through the app as before: pocketone serve --s3Redirect=false In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" app := pocketbase.New() s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) app.Start() Then turn on S3 in Settings → Files storage.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Configure
text: Set it in pocketone.yaml : s3redirect: enabled: true # false streams files through the app ttl: 5m # how long each signed URL is valid Or with flags, which win over the file: --s3Redirect true Redirect downloads when S3 file storage is on. --s3Redirect=false streams them. --s3RedirectTTL 5m How long each signed URL stays valid (at most 7 days). Keep the TTL short: anyone holding a URL can fetch the file until it expires, protected files included. The bucket itself is PocketBase's own S3 setting, in Settings → Files storage . There are no other settings screens. Bucket CORS. A redirect followed by fetch() or from your site needs a CORS rule on the bucket allowing GET from your origin. Plain , and links need nothing.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: s3redirect:
text: Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win. enabled bool On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. ttl duration How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Use
text: Once S3 is on, there's nothing to click. File URLs stay the same; they answer with a redirect: Access checks don't change. PocketBase still finds the record, checks protected-file tokens and the view rule, and creates thumbnails on first request. The redirect happens only after all of that. The file token stays private. It never goes into the bucket URL, and the redirect sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer . Same headers as PocketBase: inline or attachment ( ?download=1 ), the filename, and forced content types (SVG, CSS, JS) are signed into the URL as S3 response- overrides. Range requests work, because S3 serves them. Caching: the browser may reuse the redirect for 80% of the TTL ( Cache-Control: private , never shared caches); the file itself gets PocketBase's usual 30-day Cache-Control . Falls back to streaming when S3 is off, the plugin is turned off, or signing fails. A failed signature logs a warning, s3redirect: signing failed, streaming instead . Only GET and HEAD requests are redirected. Inline vs attachment: PocketBase decides this from the stored content type; S3 Redirect goes by the file extension (it doesn't ask the bucket, so a redirect costs no extra round trip). They agree for every file PocketBase names.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Try it
text: cd example && go run . serve The example runs one app with its own in-process bucket, nothing to set up. It: starts an S3-compatible bucket on 127.0.0.1:9199 (gofakes3, objects kept in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt ), and points the app's Files storage at it; seeds a demo_files record with an image (thumbs 100x100 ) and a protected text file, uploaded through PocketBase; prints the URLs to open. Each answers 302 to the bucket. The bucket only serves presigned GETs whose signature, re-computed with the AWS SDK's own SigV4 signer , matches and hasn't expired, and logs each one ( demo bucket: presigned GET ..., signature valid ). Unsigned or edited URLs get 403 . So a working download proves the signatures are AWS-compatible, not just accepted by a lenient fake. S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 skips the demo bucket (use your own Files storage settings); S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR moves it. The example is its own Go module, so its demo dependencies (gofakes3, the AWS SDK signer) never reach the plugin's go.mod .

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Works with
text: Pocker The same plugin runs on every instance. The s3redirect section sets the defaults; each instance can override enabled and ttl (below). S3 Fallback Apps without their own S3 settings keep files in its bucket (under pocker, fenced to instances/ /storage/ ). Its driver signs, so those downloads redirect too.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Per-instance settings (pocker)
text: srv.Plugins = append(srv.Plugins, s3redirect.New(s3redirect.Config{})) s3redirect: # server defaults enabled: true # on unless false ttl: 5m instances: id: abc plugins: s3redirect: { enabled: false } # per instance: enabled, ttl It's a pluginkit plugin, so the same value works on a single app and on every pocker instance; it doesn't link pocker.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Building on S3 Redirect
text: Supply your own bucket. S3 Redirect signs for whatever filesystem PocketBase serves the download from: the app's own S3 settings, or one a plugin supplies through OnFilesystemCreate . Implement s3redirect.Signer ( SignedURL(key, ttl, now, overrides) ) on your filesystem driver and its downloads redirect. Nothing else needs wiring; a filesystem that can't sign (local disk) streams as usual. Your own download handlers run first. The plugin binds OnFileDownloadRequest last (priority 1000, id s3redirect.HookID , __ext_s3redirect__ ), so your Go or JS handlers can still change the served file or answer themselves without calling e.Next() . Unbind the id to turn it off for one app.

title: S3 Redirect
heading: Example
text: example/main.go starts its own in-process S3 bucket, points the app's file storage at it and seeds a record, so every download redirect works with nothing to set up. Run go run . serve in example/ and open the URLs it prints. // Command example runs one PocketBase app whose file downloads redirect to an S3 bucket, with nothing to set up: // it starts its own S3-compatible bucket in-process (gofakes3, stored in pb_data/demo-s3.bolt), points the app's // Files storage at it, and seeds a "demo_files" record with an image and a protected document. // // go run . serve // // Open the URLs it prints. Each answers 302 with a signed URL; the bucket logs every fetch and only serves it if the // signature is valid and unexpired, checked independently with the AWS SDK's SigV4 signer. // // Set S3REDIRECT_DEMO=0 to skip the demo bucket and use whatever Files storage you configure in the dashboard. // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" s3redirect.MustRegister(app, s3redirect.Config{TTL: 5 time.Minute}) if os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO") != "0" { addr := os.Getenv("S3REDIRECT_DEMO_ADDR") if addr == "" { addr = "127.0.0.1:9199" } registerDemo(app, addr) } if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: S3 Redirect
heading: How it works
text: Go module github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/s3redirect , no dependencies beyond PocketOne. The redirect is an OnFileDownloadRequest handler; the hook already exists upstream, so there's no core change. Signing is SigV4 query-string auth in sigv4 , checked against AWS's documented example. It needs no change to PocketBase's S3 client. The TTL is clamped to between 1 second and 7 days.

title: Sandbox
text: Confines one PocketBase app's JS hooks and migrations, so apps from people you don't know can share one process. File access stays inside the app's folder, host primitives are gone, every JS call has a time limit, raw SQL can't leave the app's own database files, and outbound connections reach public addresses only. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Sandbox
heading: Install
text: Sandbox isn't a switch in pocketone : Pocker applies it to every instance it runs. With provider: pocker in pocketone.yaml , every instance is sandboxed and there's nothing to install. A single app served by pocketone without a provider is not sandboxed. In your own Go build, give it to PocketBase's JS plugin as an extension: sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{Dir: dir, Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}} jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{sb}, }) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox . The SQL guard and the outbound network rules are separate calls (see Integrations).

title: Sandbox
heading: Configure
text: Sandbox has no pocketone.yaml section of its own. Under Pocker its limits are set in the pocker section, as defaults for every instance, and each instance can override them in its own limits : pocker: max_js_execution: 30s # each JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after this max_js_allocation: 64MiB # biggest single allocation JS can ask for max_call_stack_size: 2000 # JS recursion depth max_sleep: 10s # cap on sleep() max_query_duration: 30s # deadline for SQL statements that have none http_send_max_timeout: 60s # cap on $http.send timeouts http_send_max_body: 10MiB # cap on $http.send response size max_concurrent_js: 16 # JS calls one instance runs at once egress_allow: [] # private networks apps may still reach, such as an internal SMTP relay The values shown are Pocker's defaults. An instance gets only its own secrets as environment. In a Go build, the same settings are Sandbox fields: Dir (required), Env , MaxExecution (default 30 s, negative turns it off), MaxSleep , MaxAllocation , MaxCallStackSize , MaxConcurrent , HTTPSendMaxTimeout , HTTPSendMaxBody , and Console to send console. output somewhere other than the process's stdout and stderr.

title: Sandbox
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to operate day to day. Hooks that stick to normal app code ( routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest) run unchanged. What changes for a hook author: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit and $filesystem.local fail with "not available on this host (sandboxed)"; $os.args is empty; process-wide Go methods such as $app.restart read as undefined . Files outside the app's folder can't be read or written, by any API, including through .. or symlinks. $os.getenv and process.env see only the app's own environment. A JS call that runs past its time limit is interrupted with an error; so is one that asks for a huge allocation. $http.send to a private or loopback address is refused. Under Pocker, console. output and hook errors go to the instance's own logs/exec.log .

title: Sandbox
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Runs every instance through the sandbox, the SQL guard and the outbound network rules, with limits from the pocker section and each instance's limits . Its attack tests are in sandbox_test.go . Host Carries the per-instance limits from instances.yaml or a mothership. Firewall Rate and concurrency limits in front of every request. Docker The alternative for untrusted apps: a container per instance instead of checks inside one process. Docker doesn't use the sandbox.

title: Sandbox
heading: Building on Sandbox
text: Sandbox is a jsvm.Extension ( OnInit , OnCall , HTTPClient ); add it to jsvm.Config.Extensions . GuardedDBConnect(maxQuery) is a core.DBConnectFunc : set it as the app's DBConnect to open the databases through SQLite's authorizer, with a deadline for statements that have none. InstallEgressPolicy(sandbox.EgressPolicy{Allow: ...}) routes Go's default HTTP transport through the public-only dialer, for the whole process. EgressPolicy.Dialer() gives the same check for your own connections. BindMail(app) sends the app's own SMTP through that dialer. ErrSandboxed is the error disabled bindings return.

title: Sandbox
heading: Example
text: One app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access confined to the app folder, host primitives disabled, and a 5 s limit per JS call. Run it from this folder with go run ./example serve . // Command example runs one PocketBase app whose JS hooks are sandboxed: file access is confined to the app folder, // host primitives ($os.exec, $os.exit, ...) are disabled, and every JS call has a time limit. // // go run ./example serve // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "os" "path/filepath" "time" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/plugins/jsvm" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/sandbox" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" dir, _ := os.Getwd() sb := &sandbox.Sandbox{ Dir: dir, // JS may only touch this folder Env: map[string]string{"GREETING": "hi"}, // the only environment JS sees MaxExecution: 5 time.Second, } jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{ HooksDir: filepath.Join(dir, "pb_hooks"), Extensions: []jsvm.Extension{sb}, // OnInit, OnCall and HTTPClient }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Sandbox
heading: How is this safe?
text: With pocker, PocketOne can serve hundreds of PocketBase instances from one Go process, each with its own owner, hooks and data. This section explains why that's safe enough to run code from people you don't know, and where it isn't. Configuration and the engine API are in POCKER.md. The attack tests are in sandbox_test.go .

title: Sandbox
heading: Why one process
text: Most hosted PocketBase instances are idle most of the time. A container per instance means paying idle memory and a cold start of a second or more for each one. In one process an instance's app starts on its first request in tens of milliseconds, costs a few MB while it runs, and shares the Go runtime with everyone else. What you give up is the kernel boundary between tenants. Everything below replaces it with checks inside the process.

title: Sandbox
heading: The threat
text: Assume every instance's owner is hostile. They control: their pb_hooks (JavaScript, run by PocketBase's goja VM); their pb_migrations ; their collections, rules and settings; any SQL their hooks run; requests to their own instance. They must not be able to: read or change another instance's files, database, environment or settings; read the host's files, environment, credentials or private network; take the process down, or starve everyone else of CPU and memory.

title: Sandbox
heading: 1. Each instance is its own PocketBase app
text: Every instance has its own core.App , database, settings, JS VMs, migrations list, settings encryption key and log. Requests are routed by hostname to exactly one app. Nothing in one app holds a reference to another. In production only hostnames the instance source maps are served; unknown hosts get 404 and never create a folder.

title: Sandbox
heading: 2. Files: confined by the kernel, not by string checks
text: Every file API reachable from JS goes through an os.Root opened on the instance's folder. That covers: $os. $filepath.glob / walk $filesystem.fileFromPath $template.loadFiles $apis.static require() The kernel resolves each path beneath that root and refuses .. and symlinks that lead out. There is no path string for an attacker to get clever with.

title: Sandbox
heading: 3. Host primitives: removed
text: The following are gone from JS: process control: $os.cmd , $os.exec , $os.exit , $os.args ; $filesystem.local ; PocketBase internals that reach the whole process: $app.restart , bootstrap , onServe , onTerminate , raw hook triggers, sql.DB handles; Go's os/exec , net , syscall and database/sql/driver . A field-name mapper hides them, so they read as undefined . Everything a normal app uses still works: routerAdd , onRecord , cronAdd , $app.findRecordById and the rest.

title: Sandbox
heading: 4. Environment: only the instance's own
text: $os.getenv and process.env return the instance's own secrets and nothing else. Platform values never go through the environment: the settings encryption key; superusers the host keeps in sync; private tokens for the host's Go code.

title: Sandbox
heading: 5. SQL: SQLite's own authorizer
text: Raw SQL is allowed ( $app.db().newQuery(...) ), because PocketBase apps depend on it. Instead of parsing statements, PocketOne installs SQLite's authorizer callback on every connection, so SQLite itself refuses: ATTACH and VACUUM INTO outside the instance's pb_data ; load_extension ; the pragmas that move SQLite's files elsewhere. Statements without a deadline get one ( max_query_duration ).

title: Sandbox
heading: 6. Outbound network: public addresses only
text: PocketOne installs one dialer process-wide, on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client. It covers: $http.send $filesystem.fileFromURL S3 storage and backups OAuth2/JWKS fetches SMTP The dialer refuses: loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata; CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges; the IPv6 forms of all of these, including IPv4-in-IPv6. It checks the address actually connected to, after DNS, so DNS rebinding doesn't help. $http.send timeouts and response sizes are capped.

title: Sandbox
heading: 7. CPU, memory and concurrency
text: CPU Every JS call (hook, route, cron, migration) is interrupted after max_js_execution . sleep() is capped. Concurrency At most max_concurrent_js JS calls per instance at once; more wait, then fail. Per-IP and per-instance rate and concurrency limits sit in front of every request. One-shot memory Built-ins that allocate a big result in one step refuse results over max_js_allocation : repeat , padStart , join , typed arrays, ArrayBuffer , Buffer , file reads and others. Recursion depth is capped, so a JS stack overflow can't crash Go. Gradual memory Not limited: goja can't account memory per VM. Gradual growth counts against the whole process (and its swap). Every limit has a process default and a per-instance override.

title: Sandbox
heading: 8. Failures stay with their instance
text: A broken hooks file, a panic during start or a failed migration fails that instance alone: it answers 502 and logs to its own logs/exec.log . Every other instance keeps serving. console. output goes to the instance's own log, never to the host's.

title: Sandbox
heading: What it doesn't cover
text: Be clear about these before you host strangers: Gradual memory isn't per instance. goja can't account memory per VM, so a hook that grows memory slowly uses the whole process's memory (and swap). Only one-shot allocations are capped. It's one address space. A bug in Go, goja, SQLite or PocketOne's own checks would cross tenants in a way a container boundary wouldn't. The sandbox tests cover the known paths, but they don't prove nothing else exists. No OS-level layer yet. Seccomp, Landlock and a second, OS-level egress filter aren't built in.

title: Sandbox
heading: How to run it
text: For untrusted tenants, add the OS layers yourself: run PocketOne as a non-root user that owns only the instances folder; run it under a cgroup memory limit (with swap), so the worst case is a restart, not a host OOM; add an OS firewall rule that lets that user reach public addresses only, an egress layer independent of the process; keep secrets for host code out of the process environment; use private: values instead; put a proxy or the built-in firewall in front, with rate limits on. If you only run your own apps, the defaults are already more than stock PocketBase gives you.

title: Server Timing
text: A Server-Timing response header on every request to a Pocker instance: how long the instance's own handler took, and how long it took to wake the instance for the request. Your browser's dev tools show it in the request's Timing tab. Server-Timing: origin;dur=12.4, wake;dur=0.0 Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Server Timing
heading: Install
text: Server Timing is built into pocketone and on whenever it serves many instances with provider: pocker . There's nothing to install. It isn't used for a single app or under provider: docker . In your own Pocker build, list it first among the plugins, so its header covers every other hop: srv := &pocker.Server{Config: cfg, Plugins: []pocker.Plugin{servertiming.New() / , other plugins /}} The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/servertiming . It works the same in pocker.Provider{Plugins: ...} .

title: Server Timing
heading: Configure
text: There's nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, flag or settings screen.

title: Server Timing
heading: Use
text: Open your browser's dev tools, pick a request to an instance and look at its timing, or read the header with curl: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/health grep -i server-timing origin The instance's own handler: from handing it the request until it sent its response headers. wake Starting the instance for this request. 0 when it was already running. Each value is in milliseconds, one decimal, up to the response headers (time to first byte). The innermost hop comes first; values a server in front already sent are kept, and this host's entries are added after them.

title: Server Timing
heading: Integrations
text: Pocker registers origin and wake for every request it hands to an instance. Add your own entries. Host code and other plugins call pocker.Timing(ctx, fn) during a request; fn returns []pocker.TimingEntry{{Name, Dur, Desc}} and runs when the headers go out. Only plugins listed after Server Timing are covered. Put names in Desc , never addresses. Go API. FormatTiming , AppendServerTiming and WithServerTiming render entries, append them to a header and wrap a response writer, for a server that isn't a Pocker plugin.

title: Server Timing
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go . See it used in examples/pocketone/multi.go , which lists it first in the pocketone binary's Pocker plugins.

title: Server Timing
heading: How it works
text: It's a Pocker wrapper ( Wrap(http.Handler) ). For each request it starts collecting timing entries in the request's context, then stamps them into the Server-Timing header just before the response headers go out (not on interim 1xx responses). Flush, Hijack and http.ResponseController keep working through its writer.

title: S3 Fallback
text: A default bucket for instances that have no S3 of their own. You name your S3-compatible backends once, then mount each kind of file on one: record uploads, backup zips, PITR history, or any plugin's own kind. Every instance gets its own folder in the bucket and can't reach anything outside it. The credentials never reach the instance. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Install
text: S3 Fallback isn't built into pocketone ; add it to a Go build. Under Pocker, add it to the server's plugins: srv := &pocker.Server{Config: cfg, Plugins: []pocker.Plugin{storage.New(storage.Config{})}} On a single app, register it with the backends and mounts in Go: pluginkit.MustRegister(app, storage.New(storage.Config{Backends: backends, Mounts: mounts})) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/storage .

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Configure
text: Under Pocker the storage section of pocketone.yaml is read at start. Fields set in Go win. storage: backends: # named S3-compatible destinations r2-eu: { endpoint: https:// .eu.r2.cloudflarestorage.com, bucket: pocketbase-eu, region: auto, access_key: $R2_KEY, secret: $R2_SECRET } b2-cold: { endpoint: ..., bucket: ph-backups, region: ..., access_key: ..., secret: ... } mounts: # filesystem kind - backend storage: r2-eu # record uploads backups: b2-cold # backup zips litestream: r2-eu # PITR history (ext/pitr) # enabled: false # off for every instance Each backend also takes prefix (prepended to every key, so several deployments can share a bucket) and force_path_style (for MinIO and similar servers). With no mounts the plugin does nothing and files stay on local disk, as in PocketBase. Each instance can turn it off in its own settings, from instances.yaml or a mothership. Only enabled is read per instance; backends and mounts are the operator's: instances: id: blog plugins: { storage: { enabled: false } } The old shape ( bucket: with uploads: / backups: ) still works, with a warning: it becomes a backend named default , mounted for uploads and backups.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Use
text: There's nothing to do day to day. To an instance nothing is configured: Settings show S3 off, and uploads, thumbs, $app.newFilesystem() and the Backups screen work as before. Files land in the bucket under instances/ / / . Downloads stream through the server, or redirect to the bucket with S3 Redirect. When an instance turns on its own S3 (Settings → Files storage, or Settings → Backups), PocketBase's normal code takes over with the instance's credentials. Files already in the default bucket stay there, as PocketBase's own S3 switch doesn't move files either. It applies to instances created with the plugin on. Files already on an instance's local disk are not read or moved.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Works with
text: Pocker Each instance gets the root instances/ / ; the storage section is read when the server starts. PITR Mount litestream and every instance without its own bucket keeps its history there. An instance's own PITR bucket still wins. S3 Redirect Downloads become signed redirects to the bucket. Nothing to wire: the fenced filesystem signs with its prefix, so S3 Redirect treats it like any S3 mount.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Building on S3 Fallback
text: Your own kind. Any kind a plugin asks for through PocketBase's OnFilesystemCreate is served when it's mounted. PITR's litestream works this way. Uploads and backups step aside when the app turned on its own S3; for other kinds, the plugin asking checks its own app setting first. Go API. Bind(app, root) serves an app's filesystems from the mounts under root ( "" for a single app, instances/ / under Pocker). FS(root, kind) returns the same fenced filesystem outside a hook; close it when done. Config() returns the effective configuration.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: Example
text: There's no example/main.go yet. storage_test.go and mounts_test.go show it on a single app and under Pocker, against MinIO.

title: S3 Fallback
heading: How it works
text: PocketBase asks OnFilesystemCreate before it creates a filesystem. For a mounted kind, the plugin answers with the backend, fenced to / . An instance can't list, read, write or delete anything outside it. The fence is a driver that adds the prefix to every key and strips it from listings. Signed download URLs are made with the backend's own credentials.

text: Works and is tested against MinIO; not yet deployed.

title: Tokens
text: Long-lived API tokens for your app: secrets that start with pbt_ , for CI, deploys, scripts and agents. Each token belongs to an account and acts as that account. It can be limited to scopes, given an expiry, and revoked on its own. Send one as Authorization: Bearer pbt_… . Ordinary PocketBase auth tokens keep working unchanged. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Tokens
heading: Install
text: Tokens is built into pocketone and always on. There's nothing to install or turn on. In your own Go build, register it before the app starts: app := pocketbase.New() tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{}) app.Start() To use $tokens in pb_hooks , bind it in jsvm's OnInit (the stock binary does): jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(vm goja.Runtime) { tokens.BindJS(vm, app) }}) The module is github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens .

title: Tokens
heading: Configure
text: There is no pocketone.yaml section, flag or environment variable for Tokens. In pocketone : any account (a superuser, or a record of any auth collection) can own tokens; a token never expires unless you give it an expiry. A Go build can narrow both (see Go config).

title: Tokens
heading: Scopes
text: A token without scopes has its owner's full rights. A token with scopes works only on the requests its scopes cover, plus /_pocker/whoami ; anywhere else it gets 403 . Plugins and your own pb_hooks register the scopes. In pocketone the built-in ones are: deploy Deploy Deploy code (hooks, migrations, public files, packages), read files and logs superusers deploy:read Deploy Read deployed files and stream logs superusers pocketone token scopes lists every scope your app has, with its paths.

title: Tokens
heading: Your own scopes
text: Declare a scope at the top level of a pb_hooks file. It then shows up in Settings → API tokens and on the OAuth Server consent page: // pb_hooks/scopes.pb.js $tokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:read', // lower-case letters, digits, ":" and "_" description: 'Read notes', // shown in the token screen and on the consent page paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'], // URL prefixes where a token holding it works methods: ['GET'], // optional: only these methods (GET covers HEAD) }) $tokens.registerScope({ name: 'notes:write', description: 'Change notes', paths: ['/api/collections/notes/records'] }) collections: ['users'] limits which accounts may hold the scope. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods and collections, so reloading hooks is safe. Two names whose headers would be the same ( notes:write and notes_write ) can't both be registered. Check a scope on your own route: routerAdd('POST', '/api/notes/archive', (e) = { / ... / }, $apis.requireAuth(), $tokens.requireScope('notes:write')) $tokens.requireScope refuses a signed-out request, and a token that doesn't hold the scope. Inside a handler, $tokens.hasScope(e, 'notes:write') tells you the same. Check a scope in a collection API rule. Every signed-in request carries X-Token-Scope- : 1 for each scope it holds, and rules read it as @request.headers.x_token_scope_ ( : becomes _ ): @request.auth.id = owner && @request.headers.x_token_scope_notes_write = "1" A PocketBase auth token or an unscoped API token holds every registered scope (except ones its collection can't hold). A scoped token holds only its own scopes. A signed-out request holds none. Headers a client sends with that prefix are always dropped, so they can't be forged. $tokens.ruleField('notes:write') returns the rule field for a name, and $tokens.scopes() lists every registered scope with its header and rule field.

title: Tokens
heading: From the dashboard
text: Open Settings → API tokens (under Access ). Only superusers see this screen. Fill in a Name . Optionally set Expires in (days) , and tick any Scopes (none means full rights). By default the token is yours. To make one for another account, fill in Owner collection (default _superusers ) and Owner (id or email) . Click Create token . Copy the token now: it's shown only once and never stored. The list shows each token's name, its first characters, owner, scopes, expiry and when it was last used (time and IP). Tokens issued by OAuth Server carry an oauth: label. Click Revoke and confirm to delete one; anything using it stops working at once. App users who aren't superusers manage their own tokens through the REST API.

title: Tokens
heading: From the command line
text: The token command works on the local data dir, like superuser , so you can set up tokens before the first serve: pocketone token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci --scope deploy --ttl 720h # prints the secret pocketone token create --collection users --record user@example.com --name script pocketone token list # every token, or one owner's with an owner flag pocketone token revoke [ ...] pocketone token revoke --all --superuser admin@example.com pocketone token scopes Pick the owner with --superuser , or --collection --record . --scope can be repeated; without --ttl the token never expires.

title: Tokens
heading: Using a token
text: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_…" https://myapp.example.com/api/collections/notes/records An invalid, revoked or expired token leaves the request signed out, like an invalid PocketBase token. A scoped token used outside its scopes gets 403 ("This API token's scopes (…) don't allow this request."). A token can't be exchanged for a PocketBase auth token ( auth-refresh and impersonate refuse it), so revoking a token really ends its access. Expired tokens are deleted once a day. Deleting an account deletes its tokens.

title: Tokens
heading: In the logs
text: A rejected token is logged at debug level: tokens: rejected API token . The daily cleanup logs tokens: deleted expired tokens with a count when it deletes any, and tokens: delete expired as a warning if it fails.

title: Tokens
heading: Works with
text: OAuth Server Its access tokens are API tokens, issued with the client's id, the granted scopes and, when asked for, an audience. They show up under Settings → API tokens and can be revoked there. OAuth Server needs Tokens on the app. MCP An agent's OAuth sign-in to /mcp is an API token bound to /mcp that never expires; revoke it to disconnect the agent. Tool calls run as the token's owner. A full-access token's calls hold every registered scope; a token limited to scopes on the consent page has its calls checked like requests with those scopes ( WithScopes ). Deploy Registers deploy and deploy:read ; a deploy token is what CI uses. Remotes A password pocketone login creates an API token and logout deletes it. In CI, put a token in POCKETONE_TOKEN (or POCKETONE_TOKEN_ ). /_pocker/whoami reports a token's id and scopes, whatever its scopes. Pocker Add tokens.New(tokens.Config{}) to the host's plugins and every instance gets its own tokens, routes and screen. Per instance, plugins: {tokens: {enabled: false}} turns it off and collections: [...] picks who may own tokens. The stock pocketone binary doesn't add it to pocker instances.

title: Tokens
heading: Building on Tokens
text: Register a scope from Go. Plugins register their scopes on the app, usually on bootstrap, and guard their routes: tk := tokens.For(app) tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{ Name: "notes:write", Description: "Change notes", Paths: []string{"/api/collections/notes/records"}, Methods: []string{"POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"}, // optional Collections: []string{"users"}, // optional: who may hold it }) se.Router.POST("/api/notes/archive", h).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("notes:write")) Guards. A Go scope can add Match func( core.RequestEvent) bool : a token with the scope also works on any request it returns true for. It runs before the owner is loaded, so it may look only at the request. Shared scopes. Registering a name again merges its paths, methods, guards and collections, so several plugins can share one scope. Read the token on a request. tokens.FromRequest(e) returns the token a request used (nil for a PocketBase auth token), with its Owner , Scopes and Audience . tokens.HasScope(e, "x") is true for PocketBase auth tokens and unscoped API tokens. Without importing this package. Read the request store keys tokens.scopes and tokens.id , or the X-Token-Scope- headers. Audience. A token created with CreateOptions.Audience (OAuth Server sets it from the RFC 8707 resource parameter) only works under that URL's path, plus /_pocker/whoami ; elsewhere it gets 403 . When the audience has a path (like https://host/mcp ), the token works there whatever its scopes: the scopes limit what that endpoint does on the token's behalf (MCP passes them on with WithScopes ), not the endpoint itself. Limit in-process requests. tokens.WithScopes(ctx, scopes) returns a context whose requests are checked like a token limited to scopes , whatever credential they carry: 403 where the scopes don't reach, and only those scopes in the X-Token-Scope- headers and HasScope . Requests made inside them with the same context inherit the limit, and a nested WithScopes only narrows it. No client value can set it. tokens.ScopesFromContext(ctx) reads it. Reaches(scopes, method, pattern) says whether scopes could cover a route pattern ( {name} segments match anything), and Scope.Infrastructure() whether a scope only reaches /_pocker/ routes. Go API. tokens.For(app) returns the service: Create(owner, CreateOptions{Name, Scopes, Expires, ClientId, Audience}) returns the secret and record; also Verify(secret) , List(owner) , Get(id) , Revoke(id) , RevokeAll(owner) , DeleteExpired() , RegisterScope , MustRegisterScope , Scopes() , Collections() and AllowedCollection(c) . tokens.BindJS(vm, app) adds $tokens ; the pluginkit plugin ( tokens.New ) also binds it. JS. $tokens.registerScope({name, description, paths, methods, collections}) , $tokens.requireScope(name) , $tokens.hasScope(e, name) , $tokens.ruleField(name) and $tokens.scopes() .

title: Tokens
heading: REST API
text: Any signed-in account; superusers see and manage everyone's. GET /api/tokens Your tokens. Superusers see all, or one owner's with ?ownerCollection=&owner= . POST /api/tokens {name, scopes, ttl \ expires} ( ttl in seconds, expires RFC 3339); superusers may add ownerCollection and owner . Returns the secret once. A scoped token can only create tokens within its own scopes. DELETE /api/tokens/{id} Revoke one. POST /api/tokens/revoke-all Revoke all of yours (superusers: {ownerCollection, owner} ). GET /api/tokens/scopes The registered scopes, who may own tokens, and whether you can. Owners can also list, view and delete their own tokens through the records API of _tokens .

title: Tokens
heading: Example
text: example/main.go runs one app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens, the /api/tokens routes and the token command. // Command example runs one PocketBase app with API tokens: Settings → API tokens in the dashboard, the /api/tokens // routes, and the token command. // // go run ./example serve // go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci // curl -H "Authorization: Bearer pbt_..." http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/collections // // Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password. package main import ( "log" "net/http" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/tokens" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password" tk := tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens }) // a plugin's scope: a token limited to "hello" only authenticates under /api/hello; a JWT or unscoped token // holds it too, and every request that holds it carries X-Token-Scope-Hello: 1 for rules and hooks tk.MustRegisterScope(tokens.Scope{Name: "hello", Description: "Say hello", Paths: []string{"/api/hello"}, Methods: []string{"GET"}}) app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se core.ServeEvent) error { se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e core.RequestEvent) error { return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]any{"hello": e.Auth.Email()}) }).Bind(apis.RequireAuth(), tokens.RequireScope("hello")) return se.Next() }) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

title: Tokens
heading: Go config
text: tokens.MustRegister(app, tokens.Config{ Collections: []string{"_superusers", "users"}, // who may own tokens (default: every auth collection) MaxTTL: 0, // cap on a token's lifetime (0: none) }) With MaxTTL set, a token asked for with no expiry or a later one gets the cap instead. If you narrow Collections , OAuth Server can only sign in accounts of those collections.

title: Tokens
heading: How it works
text: Tokens live in the _tokens collection: owner (collection id and record id), name, hash (SHA-256 of the secret; the secret itself is never stored), display prefix, scopes, expiry, last use (time and IP), OAuth client id and audience. The bearer check is a middleware that runs just before PocketBase's own auth middleware; a second one, right after it, sets the scope headers. Last use is written at most once a minute per token. example/main.go runs one app where superusers and users may own tokens, with a hello scope for GET /api/hello . Try it with go run ./example serve and go run ./example token create --superuser admin@example.com --name ci (logins from devusers: admin@example.com / password, user@example.com / password).

title: Upgrade
text: pocketone upgrade replaces the pocketone executable with the latest PocketOne release and keeps the old one beside it as - (for example pocketone-0.0.3 ), so a project can keep running the engine it was built with. Install · Configure · Use · Integrations · Example

title: Upgrade
heading: Install
text: Upgrade is built into pocketone : the upgrade command is always there. There's nothing to turn on. In your own Go build, register the command before the app starts: import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade" app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) app.Start()

title: Upgrade
heading: Configure
text: Nothing to configure: no pocketone.yaml section, no environment variables, no settings screens. The command has one flag: --backup true Back up pb_data after upgrading, if the current folder has one. --backup=false skips it.

title: Upgrade
heading: Use
text: Run it from your project folder: pocketone upgrade It: Checks the latest release on GitHub. If you already have it (or something newer), it says so and stops. Downloads the archive for your platform and checks it against the release's checksums.txt before touching anything. Renames the current executable to - and puts the new one in its place. Old copies are never deleted , so pocketone-0.0.3 serve still runs a project on that version. A local build with no release version is kept as .old , which the next such upgrade replaces. Backs up pb_data , when the current folder has one, as @upgrade_ .zip in PocketBase's backups. Prints the new version, where the old one was kept, and the release notes. Two cases where it does something else: Installed with Homebrew: it prints brew upgrade pocketone instead. Homebrew keeps the previous version until brew cleanup . In a Docker container: it refuses; upgrade the image instead. It needs write access to the folder the executable is in. A kept executable doesn't undo migrations: once a newer version has served a pb_data , an older one may not open it. The backup is the way back for that.

title: Upgrade
heading: Integrations
text: Nothing integrates with it yet. Other tools can reuse its release code: Custom builds that publish their own releases set Owner , Repo , ArchivePrefix and ArchiveExecutable in upgrade.Config . Release archives are named _ _ _ .zip , with a goreleaser-style checksums.txt in the same release. Go API. Config.FetchRelease(ctx, tag) fetches the latest release (tag "" ) or a given one; Config.DownloadArchive(ctx, release, goos, goarch, dir) downloads and checks a platform's archive. upgrade.KeptName(exe, version) is the name an old executable is kept under.

title: Upgrade
heading: Example
text: example/main.go is PocketBase plus the upgrade command. Try it with go run ./example upgrade . // Command example is PocketBase with the upgrade command. A local build has no release version, so it is kept as // "example.old"; release builds are kept as " - ". // // go run ./example upgrade package main import ( "log" "ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase" "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade" ) func main() { app := pocketbase.New() upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{}) if err := app.Start(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }
